$comment: The provenance ledger. Generated from the pages by tools/build-ledger.py; the pages remain the source of truth until the views are rewired to read this file. label_class is the canonical four-label colour; label_text is the page's own gloss, bespoke on some pages (label_canonical).

claims.title: 11B-X-1371
claims.standfirst: A short video of a masked figure with coded imagery, mailed on a DVD and posted online. The codes have been partly decoded; the purpose has not.

claims.title: The 15-Minute Lockdown
claims.standfirst: A claim that urban planning proposals are a scheme to confine people. The proposals are real; the confinement is not.

claims.title: The 1MDB Heist
claims.standfirst: Billions taken from a Malaysian state fund, traced through banks, films and a yacht. The prosecutions are documented.

claims.title: The 2008 Bailouts
claims.standfirst: Governments bought stakes in banks and insurers. The scale and the recovery are documented; the verdict is argued.

claims.title: 23andMe and Genealogy Policing
claims.standfirst: Consumer DNA databases used to identify criminal suspects through their relatives. The practice is documented and consequential.

claims.title: 5G and COVID-19
claims.standfirst: A claim that mobile networks caused or spread the disease. It led to attacks on masts and to real harm.

claims.title: The A858 Subreddit
claims.standfirst: A subreddit that posted strings of encrypted or random data for three years, with no explanation. The mystery is documented; the explanation is mundane.

claims.title: The abc Conjecture
claims.standfirst: A conjecture about the prime factors of a+b=c that would settle a family of Diophantine problems. A claimed proof has been disputed since 2012.

claims.title: Abiogenic Petroleum
claims.standfirst: Oil is not made from fossils in the way schoolbooks imply — but it is organic. The claim that it forms abiotically in the mantle has been tested for a century and has produced no commercial field.

facts.Where oil is found: Sedimentary basins, in the oil window

claims.title: Abuela as the Villain
claims.standfirst: A theory that the family matriarch is the film's antagonist. It is an interpretation of a work of animation.

claims.title: The Acámbaro Figurines
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Thousands of ceramic figures showing humans with dinosaurs, said to be ancient. The dating and the context failed.

claims.title: Acoustic Levitation
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The claim that sound could have lifted the stones of ancient monuments. Acoustic levitation is real, and it works on objects the size of a grain of rice.

claims.title: The Aestivation Hypothesis
claims.standfirst: Advanced civilisations may be asleep, waiting for the universe to cool so their computers run more efficiently. It explains the absence of aliens by predicting it, which is either elegant or unfalsifiable.

facts.Objection: Stars burn out sooner than the background cools

claims.title: AGI Timelines
claims.standfirst: Predictions for when machines match humans at everything. The record of past predictions is documented.

claims.title: The AI Box Experiment
claims.standfirst: A person role-plays an AI locked in a text-only box and tries to persuade a gatekeeper to release it. Two claimed successes are cited as evidence that containment would fail. They are anecdotes, not experiments.

claims.title: The AI Bubble
claims.standfirst: The claim that AI investment is a bubble. The spending is documented; whether it is a bubble is a forecast.

claims.title: AI Hallucination
claims.standfirst: Models produce fluent, confident falsehoods. The phenomenon is documented and its cause is argued.

claims.title: AI Existential Risk
claims.standfirst: Some of the people who build these systems put a double-digit probability on them causing catastrophe. Others with equal expertise put it near zero. Both are reasoning from the same absence of evidence.

facts.Main proponents: Bostrom, Russell, and many lab researchers
facts.Main sceptics: LeCun, and researchers focused on present harms
facts.Core claim: Misaligned, highly capable systems could be catastrophic
facts.Key weakness: No base rate; forecasts, not measurements

claims.title: The Aiud Wedge
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: An aluminium wedge was found in Romania in 1973 alongside bones, and was said to be ancient. Aluminium of that kind was not made before the nineteenth century, and the object is probably wartime debris.

facts.Association: Unverified fossil bones in the same sand

claims.title: The Akashic Records
claims.standfirst: A compendium of everything that has ever happened, said to be readable by the trained. It is a claim with no evidence, no mechanism and no test — and it shaped a great deal of modern spiritual writing.

facts.Claim: A universal record, readable by the trained
facts.Medium: None proposed that can be examined
facts.Test: None — errors are attributed to the reader

claims.title: Akhenaten's Revolution
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: One pharaoh replaced Egypt's gods with a single sun disc, moved the capital, and changed the art. The revolution is documented; why it happened is not.

claims.title: Al-Jazari's Automata
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A book of machines — clocks, water-raising devices and automata — with drawings clear enough to rebuild. The book survives.

claims.title: Alcohol Kills Brain Cells
claims.standfirst: Heavy drinking damages the brain. The mechanism is not the death of cells in the way the phrase suggests.

facts.Reality: Damage to dendrites and white matter

claims.title: Alexander's Lost Tomb
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Alexander the Great died in Babylon and his body was taken to Egypt. His tomb was visited for centuries, and it has never been found.

claims.title: Alexander Poisoned
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Did Alexander the Great die of disease or poison? The sources disagree and the body is lost.

claims.title: Algorithmic Fairness
claims.standfirst: In 2016 three papers proved, within months of each other, that several intuitive definitions of fairness cannot hold together. The field has been arguing about what to do with that ever since.

facts.You can have: At most two, when base rates differ

claims.title: Algorithmic Radicalisation
claims.standfirst: The claim that recommendation systems push people toward extremes. The mechanism is plausible, the evidence is thinner than the headlines, and the platform data that would settle it is not available.

claims.title: Alien Hand Syndrome
claims.standfirst: A hand that acts on its own — unbuttoning a shirt, grabbing a tool, resisting the other hand — is a real consequence of damage to the connections between the hemispheres.

facts.Agency: Intact sense that the hand is theirs, not that they control it

claims.title: Aliens, Area 51 & the UFO Files
claims.standfirst: The United States government spent twenty-two years investigating flying saucers, catalogued 12,618 sightings, and left 701 unexplained. That is a real number, and it means less than it sounds.

claims.title: The Alignment Tax
claims.standfirst: Safety measures are said to cost capability. The size of the cost is argued and measured differently.

claims.title: The Alkaline Diet
claims.standfirst: The claim that food changes blood pH and that acidity causes disease. The body regulates pH within a narrow range.

claims.title: Alzheimer's
claims.standfirst: The leading theory of Alzheimer's produced drugs that mostly failed, then two that worked slightly. That combination is more informative than either a vindication or a debunking.

facts.Fraud claim: One 2006 paper retracted, not the field

claims.title: The Amazons
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Greek writers described warrior women. Archaeology has found women buried with weapons on the steppe.

claims.title: The Amber Room
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A room panelled in amber, looted by the Nazis in 1941, and lost in 1945. The reconstruction is finished; the original is still missing, and the search has produced a great deal of theory and no amber.

facts.Original: Never found; destruction is the leading account

claims.title: AMOC Collapse
claims.standfirst: The Atlantic overturning circulation may weaken or collapse. The physics is documented; the timing and likelihood are argued.

claims.title: AMOC Tipping
claims.standfirst: The Gulf Stream is not a conveyor belt that can simply switch off, but the Atlantic overturning that carries heat north is weakening. How far, how fast, and whether it collapses is unsettled.

facts.Trend: Likely weakening; proxies suggest a century-scale decline
facts.Impact: Regional cooling, rainfall shifts, sea level

claims.title: Amyloid and Alzheimer's
claims.standfirst: The amyloid cascade hypothesis has driven thirty years of Alzheimer's research. Two drugs now remove amyloid and slow decline slightly; whether that vindicates the hypothesis is still argued.

facts.Effect: Slowed decline, roughly a quarter to a third on standard scales
facts.Risks: Brain swelling and bleeding in a minority
facts.Contested: Whether amyloid is cause or marker

claims.title: Did Anastasia Survive?
claims.standfirst: The most famous survivor story of the twentieth century, sustained by a woman who may have believed it herself, and ended by a blood sample taken from a British prince.

claims.title: Ancient Astronauts
claims.standfirst: The theory is not that ancient people were stupid. It is that they were clever enough to describe spacecraft, and that archaeologists have been reading the descriptions wrong.

facts.Key exhibits: Palenque, Nazca, Puma Punku, Dogon, crystal skulls

claims.title: Andrew Carlssin
claims.standfirst: A story about a man who turned $800 into $350 million and claimed to be a time traveller. It ran in a supermarket tabloid.

claims.title: Animal Crossing After Humans
claims.standfirst: A theory that the game is set after humanity. It is a reading of a fiction, and the game is cheerful.

claims.title: Animal Crossing Is a Cult
claims.standfirst: The joke theory that the game's cheerful village is a coercive community. It is a reading of the game's mechanics, and the game's designers did not intend it.

claims.title: How Animals Sense Magnetism
claims.standfirst: Birds, turtles and bacteria navigate by the Earth's field. The mechanism is still argued.

claims.title: The Anthropocene
claims.standfirst: Humans have changed the rock record. Whether that deserves a place in the geological timescale was put to a vote in 2024 and lost — and the vote is more interesting than the answer.

facts.IUGS decision: Rejected as a formal epoch, March 2024

claims.title: The Antikythera Mechanism
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A bronze gear mechanism from a Roman-era shipwreck, built to model the heavens. Nothing of comparable complexity appears for a thousand years afterwards.

claims.title: The Anunnaki
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Sitchin's claim that alien visitors created humanity, built on a mistranslation of Sumerian texts.

claims.title: Aphantasia
claims.standfirst: Some people close their eyes and see nothing. The condition was described in 1880, named in 2015, and is now the best-studied example of how differently ordinary minds are furnished.

facts.Objective markers: Reduced imagery priming in binocular rivalry; weaker frontal–visual coupling

claims.title: The Apkallu
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Assyrian reliefs show fish-cloaked and bird-headed sages who brought the arts to humanity. They are the Mesopotamian originals behind Oannes, and they are mythological advisers, not visitors.

facts.Depicted: Fish cloak or bird head, with bucket and cone

claims.title: The Aquatic Ape
claims.standfirst: A human ancestor that took to the water would explain hairlessness, upright posture and the diving reflex in one stroke. The fossil record, the comparative anatomy and the genetics each say otherwise, and the charitable version of the idea is a different claim.

facts.Proposed: Alister Hardy, 1960; popularised by Elaine Morgan, 1972

claims.title: Archimedes' Heat Ray
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Mirrors on the walls of Syracuse, focusing sunlight onto Roman ships. The story is late, the physics is marginal, and the experiments have produced smoke and no fire.

facts.Demonstrated: Short range, stationary target, many mirrors
facts.Conclusion: Possible in principle; unlikely in practice

claims.title: Aristarchus Put the Sun at the Centre
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A Greek astronomer proposed a heliocentric system eighteen centuries before Copernicus. The report survives, and the idea was rejected.

claims.title: The Ark as a Capacitor
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Ark of the Covenant was a gold-plated box that killed a man who touched it. The claim is that it was an electrical capacitor. The description fits a capacitor; the rest does not.

facts.Object: Gold over acacia wood, with a lid

claims.title: The Ark in the King's Chamber
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that the Ark of the Covenant was housed in the Great Pyramid. The chamber is real; the Ark is not there.

facts.Claim: The Ark was kept in the pyramid

claims.title: The Ark in Ethiopia
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A church in Aksum claims to hold the Ark of the Covenant. The claim is a matter of faith, and no examination has been permitted.

claims.title: Armstrong's Doping Programme
claims.standfirst: A seven-time winner stripped of his titles after a doping investigation and a confession.

claims.title: The Arrow of Time
claims.standfirst: Every fundamental law of physics works the same played backwards. Cups break and do not unbreak. The asymmetry is real, and it is not in the equations.

facts.Main gap: Why the early universe was so special

claims.title: Arson Myths
claims.standfirst: Investigators read patterns in fire damage as proof of arson. Many of the signs were normal fire behaviour.

claims.title: Arthur as a Roman Commander
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The earliest mention of Arthur is a battle list written three centuries after he supposedly lived. The claim that he was a Roman officer is a modern attempt to fill the gap.

claims.title: Aryabhata's Rotation
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A fifth-century astronomer stated that the Earth rotates. The text is real and the claim is in it.

claims.title: The Aryan Migration
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Who composed the Vedas, and where did they come from? The genetics and the texts are both real, and the argument is political.

claims.title: Asbestos and Radon Cover-Ups
claims.standfirst: Both asbestos and radon were known hazards long before they were regulated, and in both cases industry documents show the knowledge preceded the action.

claims.title: Ashley Madison's Bots
claims.standfirst: A dating site whose user base included large numbers of fabricated female profiles. The data leak made it measurable.

claims.title: AshVlogs
claims.standfirst: A YouTube channel presented as a missing person's video diary. It is fiction, and it was built to be mistaken for real.

claims.title: Aspartame and Cancer
claims.standfirst: A sweetener classified as possibly carcinogenic, and the dose that matters.

claims.title: Assembly Theory
claims.standfirst: A proposed measure of how complex an object is, by counting the minimum steps needed to build it. Its authors argue it explains selection and can detect life; its critics argue it measures construction, not causation.

facts.Criticism: Measures construction, not history; method contested

claims.title: The Astros Sign Stealing
claims.standfirst: A baseball team used a camera and a monitor to relay the opposing catcher's signals. The scheme is documented in a league report.

claims.title: Atlantis in Antarctica
claims.standfirst: The claim that Atlantis was Antarctica, shifted to the pole by a crustal displacement. Plate tectonics does not permit it, and the ice cores are older than the claim requires.

facts.Ice record: Continuous for hundreds of thousands of years

claims.title: Atlantis at Doñana
claims.standfirst: A team argued that Atlantis lies under the marshes of Doñana in southern Spain, destroyed by a tsunami. The site has structures, and the identification is not accepted.

claims.title: Atlantis as Thera
claims.standfirst: The Minoan eruption of Santorini destroyed a civilisation, and the parallel with Plato's story is striking. The date is the problem: it is 9,000 years out.

facts.Proposed fix: Unit error or copying error — unsupported

claims.title: Attack on Titan's Time Loop
claims.standfirst: A theory that the story repeats. It is an interpretation of a manga and anime.

claims.title: Avril Lavigne Was Replaced
claims.standfirst: A claim that the singer died in 2003 and was replaced by a body double named Melissa. The evidence is photographs, and the photographs are of the same person at different ages.

claims.title: The Axis of Evil
claims.standfirst: A pattern in the cosmic microwave background that seems to align with the solar system. It is probably a statistical artefact.

claims.title: Aztlán in Utah
claims.standfirst: A claim that the Mexica homeland was in Utah. The tradition is real; the location is not.

claims.title: Aztlán
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The ancestral homeland of the Mexica, described in colonial sources and located nowhere.

claims.title: The Baader–Meinhof Effect
claims.standfirst: Learn a new word and it appears everywhere for a week. Nothing has changed except your attention — which is why it is also called the frequency illusion.

facts.Named: 1994, in a newspaper letter; 'frequency illusion' by Zwicky, 2005

claims.title: Baalbek and the Giants
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Roman temple platform at Baalbek contains three stones of about 800 tonnes each. They were quarried, moved and set by Roman engineers, and the claim that only giants could have done it is an argument from incredulity with a documented answer.

facts.Largest blocks: About 800 tonnes each in the trilithon
facts.Still in the quarry: The Stone of the Pregnant Woman, ~1,000 t
facts.Period: Roman, on an earlier sanctuary site

claims.title: Babel as a Spaceport
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Tower of Babel is a story about language. A modern reading makes it a rocket launch facility, which requires ignoring what the text says and what Babylon actually built.

claims.title: Babylonian Trigonometry
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A clay tablet of Pythagorean triples, interpreted in 2017 as the world's oldest trigonometric table.

claims.title: Backmasking
claims.standfirst: The claim that rock records contain hidden messages played backwards. The messages are found by the listener, not put there.

claims.title: The Backrooms Levels
claims.standfirst: An endless maze of yellow rooms, invented in a 2019 forum post, expanded by thousands of writers and filmmakers. It is fiction, it is labelled, and it has become one of the defining images of the internet's sense of place.

claims.title: The Backrooms
claims.standfirst: Noclip out of reality in the wrong place and you fall into six hundred million square miles of damp carpet and buzzing lights. It began as one photograph and one paragraph.

claims.title: The Baghdad Battery
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A clay jar with a copper cylinder and an iron rod will produce a voltage if you fill it with vinegar. Whether anyone in Parthian Iraq did that is a different question, and the answer is almost certainly no.

facts.Better explanation: A scroll container, a known Parthian type

claims.title: Ball Lightning
claims.theme: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained
claims.standfirst: Glowing spheres that drift through rooms during thunderstorms have been reported for four centuries, filmed once, and measured spectroscopically in a handful of cases. The reports are too consistent to dismiss and too rare to pin down.

facts.Leading model: Vaporised soil condensing into glowing nanoparticles

claims.title: Ballistics Matching
claims.standfirst: Marks on bullets and casings are matched to a gun. The marks are real; the certainty is argued.

claims.title: The Barabar Caves
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Caves cut into granite in Bihar with polished surfaces and an echo that lasts for seconds. They were made for an ascetic sect, and the finish is documented.

claims.title: Barbie's Red Pill
claims.standfirst: A reading of a film through a phrase from an unrelated film. It is an interpretation, not a claim.

claims.title: The Basques
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A people with a language unrelated to any other in Europe, and a genetic history that is distinctive without being separate.

claims.title: The Bat Creek Stone
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A stone with an inscription said to be Hebrew, found in a Tennessee mound. It is a nineteenth-century inscription, and it is upside down.

claims.title: Batterygate
claims.standfirst: Apple slowed down older iPhones to stop them shutting down unexpectedly, and did not tell anyone. It was a reasonable engineering decision and a serious communication failure.

claims.title: BCCI
claims.standfirst: A bank grew into a global institution by serving dictators, arms dealers and intelligence services, and was closed by regulators in 1991. It is the largest bank fraud prosecuted to that date.

claims.title: Beal's Conjecture
claims.standfirst: If aˣ + bʸ = cᶻ with exponents above two, the three bases share a prime factor. There is a million-dollar prize and no proof.

facts.Statement: aˣ + bʸ = cᶻ implies a shared prime factor

claims.title: Benchmark Contamination
claims.standfirst: Test sets end up in training data, so the scores measure memory. The problem is documented and hard to fix.

claims.title: The Berenstain Bears
claims.standfirst: A generation remembers the books as 'Berenstein'. They were always 'Berenstain'. The spelling is the archive's neatest case of a false memory shared by thousands of people.

facts.Mechanism: Memory regularisation to a common surname ending

claims.title: Beringia
claims.standfirst: A land bridge between Asia and America, exposed when sea levels fell. It was not just a corridor: people lived on it for thousands of years.

facts.Region: Northeast Asia to northwest North America
facts.Now: Under the Bering and Chukchi seas

claims.title: The Bermuda Triangle
claims.theme: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained
claims.standfirst: Ships and aircraft have been lost in the western Atlantic, as they have been lost everywhere. The triangle was assembled from a handful of famous cases, a bestseller, and an absence of denominator.

facts.The error: No denominator — a busy region has more losses

claims.title: The Betz Sphere
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A steel sphere found after a forest fire was said to move on its own, hum, and resist investigation. It is a ball bearing from industrial machinery.

claims.title: The Bhavishya Purana
claims.standfirst: A purana cited for prophecies about later figures. Its predictive sections have a documented history of insertion.

claims.title: The Bicameral Mind
claims.standfirst: Three thousand years ago, humans had no inner life. Their own thoughts arrived as the voices of gods, and they obeyed them. It is one of the most audacious books of the century, and the neuroscience does not support it.

facts.Author: Julian Jaynes, 1976
facts.What survives: The history of the self as a field

claims.title: The Big Bounce
claims.standfirst: If the universe contracts before it expands, the Big Bang is not a beginning. The idea is mathematically developed and observationally untested, and the cosmic microwave background is where it would show.

claims.title: The Big Mac Index
claims.standfirst: A burger as a currency benchmark. It is a joke that works as a teaching tool and not as a forecast.

claims.title: Bilderberg
claims.standfirst: An annual off-the-record meeting of politicians, bankers and executives. It is real, it is influential, and it is not secret — the participant list is published every year.

claims.title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer
claims.standfirst: A conjecture connecting the number of rational points on an elliptic curve to a function attached to it. It is the Millennium problem with the most computational support.

facts.Claim: Rank equals the order of vanishing

claims.title: The Quantum Biology of the Bird Compass
claims.standfirst: Migratory birds navigate using the Earth's magnetic field, and the leading explanation involves quantum entanglement in a protein in the retina. It is one of the best-supported examples of quantum biology.

claims.title: Bitcoin as Digital Gold
claims.standfirst: The white paper proposed a peer-to-peer electronic cash system. Fifteen years later its main use is as an asset whose price is quoted in the currency it was meant to replace.

claims.title: Bite Mark Evidence
claims.standfirst: Dentists testified that a wound matched a suspect's teeth. The science was never validated, and people were convicted.

claims.title: The Black Hole Information Paradox
claims.standfirst: Hawking radiation carries no information about what fell in. If that is true, quantum mechanics is wrong; if it is false, relativity is. Fifty years of work has produced progress and no experiment.

facts.Progress: Holography; the island formula; the Page curve
facts.Obstacle: No full theory of quantum gravity

claims.title: The Black Knight
claims.standfirst: An alien satellite in polar orbit for 13,000 years, photographed by NASA in 1998. The photograph is real. The object is a piece of insulation that drifted out of the shuttle's cargo bay.

claims.title: Black Mirror's One Timeline
claims.standfirst: A theory that every episode shares a single timeline. It is an interpretation of an anthology series.

claims.title: The Black Sea Deluge
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A hypothesis that the Black Sea flooded catastrophically when the Mediterranean broke through. The flood is argued; its scale and date are not settled.

claims.title: Black Swans
claims.standfirst: Nobody predicted 2008, the pandemic or the smartphone. The interesting question is not that surprises happen but whether our models are built to be surprised by them.

claims.title: Block Universe or Growing Block
claims.standfirst: Does time pass, or is the universe a four-dimensional block in which all moments exist? Physics constrains the answer without settling it.

claims.title: Bloodletting
claims.standfirst: The standard treatment for almost everything, practised for two thousand years, and harmful.

claims.title: Bloodstain Pattern Analysis
claims.standfirst: The shapes of bloodstains are used to reconstruct events. The physics is real; the inferences are argued.

claims.title: Blue Light and Circadian Damage
claims.standfirst: Short-wavelength light suppresses melatonin and shifts the body clock. That much is solid. The claim that screens damage the retina, or that blue-blocking glasses fix sleep, is where the evidence thins out.

claims.title: The Blue Whale Challenge
claims.standfirst: A supposed game that assigned self-harm tasks. No evidence of the game has been found; the panic caused real harm.

claims.title: Boeing's MCAS
claims.standfirst: A software system designed to correct a handling characteristic, fed by a single sensor, brought down two aircraft. 346 people died.

claims.title: The Bog Bodies
claims.standfirst: Hundreds of bodies have been recovered from northern European peat bogs, preserved by the chemistry of the peat. Many were killed deliberately.

claims.title: BoJack Drowned
claims.standfirst: A theory that the horse died in a swimming pool and the rest of the series is his dying imagination. It is a reading of a show about a character who nearly dies.

claims.title: Boltzmann Brains
claims.standfirst: If the universe fluctuates forever, a random self-aware brain with false memories is far more likely than an entire ordered cosmos. Nobody thinks that means you are one. It means something is wrong with the model.

facts.Claim: A model filter, not a biography

claims.title: The Boötes Void
claims.standfirst: A region of sky about 330 million light years across contains far fewer galaxies than it should. It is real, it is not empty, and it is not evidence of anything stranger than large-scale structure.

facts.Contents: Galaxies, at well below average density
facts.Not supported: That it is empty, or artificial

claims.title: The Boring Billion
claims.standfirst: Between about 1.8 and 0.8 billion years ago, the Earth's climate, oceans and evolution appear to have been unusually stable. Whether it was boring is now disputed.

claims.title: The Bosnian Pyramids
claims.standfirst: Four hills near Visoko, said to be the largest human-made pyramids on Earth, older than Sumer. The shape is real. The construction is not.

claims.title: The Bowery's Hidden Army
claims.standfirst: A theory about a hidden faction in a game's city. It is an interpretation of a fiction.

facts.Claim: A cut faction remains in the world

claims.title: The Brahmastra
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Mahabharata describes celestial weapons of enormous destructive power. They have been read as nuclear bombs. They are literary devices in a poem about dharma.

claims.title: Brain-Computer Hive Minds
claims.standfirst: The claim that brain-computer interfaces will merge people into a collective intelligence. The interfaces are real; the hive is not.

claims.title: Brain Training
claims.standfirst: Games said to make you smarter. You get better at the games.

claims.title: Brandolini's Law
claims.standfirst: The energy needed to refute nonsense is an order of magnitude greater than the energy needed to produce it. It is the reason this archive exists in the form it does.

facts.Claim: Refutation costs an order of magnitude more

claims.title: Breaking Bad and The Walking Dead
claims.standfirst: A theory that the two shows share a universe, built on a bag of blue meth and a timeline. It is a joke that got elaborate.

claims.title: Britney's Coded Posts
claims.standfirst: A claim that a celebrity's social media posts contain hidden messages. The reading is a community's, and the code is not established.

claims.title: Broken Windows Policing
claims.standfirst: An essay in The Atlantic in 1982 argued that untended disorder invites serious crime. It became the operating theory of American policing, and then it was tested.

facts.Systematic reviews: Small disorder effects; little on serious crime
facts.Court ruling: Floyd v. City of New York, 2013

claims.title: Bullshit Jobs
claims.standfirst: David Graeber's claim that a large share of jobs are pointless and their holders know it. The essay struck a nerve; the survey evidence is thinner than the argument.

facts.Author: David Graeber
facts.Claim: Many jobs are pointless, and holders know

claims.title: Burrows Cave
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A cave in Illinois said to hold thousands of inscribed stones from lost civilisations. The cave has never been shown to anyone.

claims.title: Cadaver Dogs
claims.standfirst: Dogs trained to find human remains. The capability is real and the reliability is variable.

claims.title: Cahokia's Emptying
claims.standfirst: The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, abandoned within two centuries. Its population and its end are both argued.

claims.title: Caligula's Horse
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The emperor was said to have made his horse a consul. The sources are hostile, and the story is probably a joke about a private plan.

facts.Claim: The horse was to be made consul
facts.Likely reading: A joke or threat taken literally

claims.title: The Call of the Void
claims.standfirst: Standing at a height, a small number of people feel a sudden urge to jump. It is not a death wish, it is common, and it has a name in French that predates the research.

facts.Name: L'appel du vide; 'high-place phenomenon'
facts.Note: Not the same as suicidal ideation

claims.title: The Cambrian Explosion
claims.standfirst: Almost every major animal group appears in the fossil record within about twenty million years. Whether that is an explosion of life or an explosion of fossils is the argument, and it has been running since Darwin apologised for it.

facts.Key sites: Burgess Shale (1909); Chengjiang; Emu Bay Shale
facts.What appeared: Most major animal phyla, in mineralised form
facts.The argument: A real radiation, or a real radiation plus a better record

claims.title: Cambridge Analytica
claims.standfirst: A political consulting firm obtained Facebook data on millions of users through a personality quiz app, and used it for targeted advertising. The scandal changed how the platform handled data.

claims.title: Cancer's Origin
claims.standfirst: Cancer is not one disease but a process: cells evolving inside a body, escaping the controls that make multicellular life possible. That framing explains more than any single cause does.

facts.Not established: A single cause or a general cure

claims.title: Canon Events
claims.standfirst: The idea that a story's fixed events must happen, used in a film and discussed as a rule of fiction.

claims.title: Cantre'r Gwaelod
claims.standfirst: A drowned kingdom under Cardigan Bay, kept out by a gate that was left open. The legend is real; the kingdom is not.

claims.title: Capitalist Realism
claims.standfirst: Mark Fisher's argument that capitalism has become the horizon of thought, so that alternatives are unimaginable. It is a diagnosis, not a measurement.

facts.Author: Mark Fisher
facts.Claim: Capitalism is the horizon of thought

claims.title: The Carbohydrate–Insulin Model
claims.standfirst: The claim that obesity is driven by insulin, and that carbohydrate restriction is therefore uniquely effective. The trials find that, matched for protein and calories, the diets perform similarly.

facts.Claim: Insulin drives fat storage; carbs cause obesity
facts.Short-term: Low-carb diets show greater early loss
facts.Prediction: Insulin resistance should predict response — it does not

claims.title: Carnac as a Seismograph
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that the Carnac stones were arranged to record earthquakes. The rows are real; the function is invented.

claims.title: Cars Wiped Out Humanity
claims.standfirst: A Pixar shared-universe theory in which the cars inherited a world the humans left. It is a joke, and the films do not say it.

claims.title: Catharsis
claims.standfirst: The idea that venting anger relieves it. The evidence says the opposite: rehearsal makes anger more accessible, and the studies that tested it found venting increases aggression.

claims.title: Cattle Mutilations
claims.standfirst: Cattle found dead with clean cuts and missing organs, said to be the work of something unusual. The forensic explanations are ordinary and varied.

claims.title: The CE5 Contact Protocol
claims.standfirst: Paid events where groups meditate to summon UFOs. Participants report lights in the sky; the lights are usually identifiable, and the protocol has never produced an object anyone could examine.

facts.Term: Close encounter of the fifth kind
facts.Method: Meditation and light signalling at night

claims.title: Celebrity Vampire Tintypes
claims.standfirst: Photographs said to show famous people as vampires. They are digital composites made to look like old photographs.

claims.title: Chaco's Straight Roads
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Hundreds of kilometres of roads radiating from Chaco Canyon, built straight and often ending nowhere.

claims.title: Chavín's Psychedelic Gods
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The stone carvings at Chavín de Huántar show fanged deities, serpents and transformations. The visionary imagery is real, and the argument that the site's rituals used hallucinogens is supported by archaeological finds.

claims.title: Chavín Gold Plating
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A culture that plated copper with gold using electrochemical methods, or so the claim goes. The objects are real; the method is argued.

claims.title: The Chemical Imbalance Critique
claims.standfirst: The claim that mental illness is caused by a chemical imbalance was told to patients for decades. It was a simplification, and the correction has been widely misread.

claims.title: Chemtrails
claims.standfirst: The claim that aircraft are spraying chemicals to control populations or climate. The trails are ice crystals, they behave exactly as contrail physics predicts, and no sampling has found the chemicals.

claims.title: Chernobyl's Design Flaw
claims.standfirst: A reactor that became unstable at low power, operated outside its limits, with a test that went wrong.

claims.title: Chewing Gum Takes Seven Years
claims.standfirst: Swallowed gum passes through in days. The seven-year figure is folklore.

claims.title: The Chimera
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A lion with a goat's head and a serpent's tail, and a possible origin in volcanic landscape.

claims.title: The Chinese Word for Crisis
claims.standfirst: The claim that 'crisis' in Chinese means danger plus opportunity. It does not.

claims.title: Chinese Gunpowder Weapons
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Gunpowder was formulated in China for medicine and fireworks, and by the Song dynasty it was a weapon.

claims.title: The Chinese Room
claims.standfirst: A person in a room follows rules for manipulating Chinese characters and produces perfect answers in Chinese. She understands nothing. Is the room a computer, or is this a story about what it feels like to be one?

facts.Target: Strong AI: the program is the mind
facts.Live consequence: Whether grounding is required for meaning

claims.title: Chip-chan
claims.standfirst: A cat that appeared in hundreds of forum images, posted by a user who later explained the story.

claims.title: Chronic Lyme
claims.standfirst: Some patients have persistent symptoms after treated Lyme disease. Whether that is an ongoing infection is the argument, and the trials have not supported prolonged antibiotics.

claims.title: Chronostasis
claims.standfirst: Glance at a clock and the first second seems to last longer. The clock is fine; your brain is filling a gap it never recorded.

claims.title: The Chupacabra
claims.standfirst: A creature that drains livestock of blood, first reported in Puerto Rico in 1995. Every carcass that has been tested has turned out to be a coyote or dog with mange.

claims.title: CIA Black Sites
claims.standfirst: The CIA ran a network of secret prisons in several countries, where detainees were held and subjected to techniques the US government later acknowledged as torture.

claims.title: The CIA–Mafia Plots Against Castro
claims.standfirst: The CIA recruited mafia figures to kill Fidel Castro, using poison pills, exploding cigars and a contaminated diving suit. The schemes failed, and the Church Committee published them.

claims.title: The CIA and Modern Art
claims.standfirst: The CIA covertly funded abstract expressionist exhibitions and journals during the Cold War, as cultural diplomacy. The paintings were real; the funding was hidden.

facts.Purpose: Cultural diplomacy in the Cold War
facts.Claim: That the CIA invented the movement — not supported

claims.title: The Circleville Letters
claims.standfirst: A small Ohio town received anonymous letters accusing residents of affairs and worse. One man was convicted of a related crime; the letter-writer was never identified.

claims.title: Cleopatra's Pearl
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The story that Cleopatra dissolved a pearl in vinegar to win a bet. The chemistry is doubtful and the source is late.

claims.title: Cleopatra at Taposiris Magna
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A temple site west of Alexandria has produced coins and a tunnel, and a claim that it holds Cleopatra's tomb. The excavator believes it; most Egyptologists are cautious.

claims.title: Clockman
claims.standfirst: A short animation remembered by a viewer and identified years later. It is a lost-media success, and the memory turned out to be accurate.

claims.title: Cloud Feedback
claims.standfirst: Clouds both warm and cool the planet, and how they will change is the largest single uncertainty in climate projection. The sign is agreed; the size is not.

claims.title: Cobb's Real Totem
claims.standfirst: In Inception, Cobb spins a top to test reality — but the top was Mal's, not his. His actual totem is his wedding ring, which appears only in dreams.

claims.title: The Coelacanth
claims.standfirst: A fish known only from fossils, and thought extinct for 65 million years, was caught off South Africa in 1938. A second population was found in Indonesia in 1997.

claims.title: Cold Fusion
claims.theme: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained
claims.standfirst: Two electrochemists announced tabletop fusion on 23 March 1989. Within six months the effect had failed to replicate, and thirty-seven years later there is still a conference, a journal and no accepted mechanism.

facts.Replication: Widespread failure of the by-product signature

claims.title: The Collatz Conjecture
claims.standfirst: Halve even numbers, triple-and-add-one odd ones, and you always reach 1. Nobody knows why, and Paul Erdős said mathematics is not ready for it.

claims.title: Collective Effervescence
claims.standfirst: Durkheim's term for what happens when a crowd assembles and feels something together. It is not mysticism; it is the mechanism by which rituals make beliefs feel true.

facts.What it is: Heightened shared emotion in assembled groups
facts.Function: Binds the group; makes beliefs feel sacred

claims.title: Collective Intelligence
claims.standfirst: The claim that groups have a measurable general intelligence, predicting performance across tasks. The original study was striking; the replications are mixed.

facts.Claim: A general factor for group performance

claims.title: The Comic Book Panic
claims.standfirst: Comic books were blamed for juvenile delinquency, and a Senate subcommittee and an industry code followed.

claims.title: Comparative Advantage
claims.standfirst: The clearest idea in economics, and the one most often misstated.

claims.title: Compute Governance
claims.standfirst: Controlling access to training compute as a way to govern AI. The policy is documented; its effectiveness is argued.

claims.title: Conformal Cyclic Cosmology
claims.standfirst: Penrose's proposal that the universe repeats, with each aeon's end becoming the next one's beginning. It makes a specific prediction about the microwave background, and the searches for it have not found it.

claims.title: Constants That Drift
claims.standfirst: The proposal that the constants of nature may vary over cosmic time. Measurements keep finding no change, to extraordinary precision.

claims.title: Constructor Theory
claims.standfirst: David Deutsch's proposal to rebuild physics around which transformations are possible, rather than around initial conditions.

claims.title: The Contact Hypothesis
claims.standfirst: Intergroup contact reduces prejudice — one of the most replicated findings in social psychology. The dispute is about the conditions: equal status, shared goals, cooperation and institutional support, all of which are easy to state and hard to arrange.

facts.Conditions: Equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support

claims.title: The Copper Scroll
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: One Dead Sea Scroll is not a text but a treasure map: sixty-four locations, quantities of gold and silver, and no treasure ever found. It is the only scroll in the collection that reads like an inventory.

claims.title: Coral Castle
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: One man carved and moved over a thousand tonnes of coral rock alone, at night, and refused to say how. The answer is levers, pulleys and patience.

claims.title: Coronil
claims.standfirst: An ayurvedic preparation launched as a COVID-19 treatment, and the regulatory record around it.

facts.Regulator: Direction to stop advertising as a cure

claims.title: Cosmic Censorship
claims.standfirst: General relativity allows singularities with no event horizon — naked points where physics stops and the universe can be seen to break. Penrose conjectured they cannot form. Nobody has proved it.

facts.Status: Unproved; Nobel 2020 was for the theorems
facts.Strong version: No observer meets a singularity at all
facts.Evidence: Numerical collapse; the Kerr spin limit

claims.title: The Cosmic Web and the Brain
claims.standfirst: A 2020 paper compared the distribution of galaxies to the network of neurons in a brain, and found them quantitatively similar. The comparison is a real result about structure, not about consciousness.

claims.title: The Coso Artifact
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A 'geode' from California was found to contain a spark plug. It was said to be half a million years old. It is a 1920s Champion spark plug in a concretion.

claims.title: The Cottingley Fairies
claims.theme: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained
claims.standfirst: Two girls photographed fairies in a Yorkshire garden, and Sherlock Holmes's creator believed them. Sixty years later they admitted the fairies were paper cut-outs pinned to a bush.

claims.title: Cow Urine as Medicine
claims.standfirst: A traditional preparation promoted as a cure, and tested. The tests do not support the claims.

claims.title: Cracking Knuckles Causes Arthritis
claims.standfirst: A doctor cracked the knuckles of one hand for sixty years. The other hand was the control.

claims.title: Creationism and the Alternatives to Darwin
claims.label_text: Settled on descent, open on mechanism
claims.standfirst: Common ancestry is about as well supported as anything in science. How evolution works in detail is still argued about — by biologists. This page separates the two, claim by claim, without pretending the argument is even.

facts.Label: Core settled
facts.Genuinely open: Origin of life; tempo; drift; genome function

claims.title: The Crooked Forest
claims.standfirst: About four hundred pines near Gryfino in Poland bend sharply north at their base. They were planted in the 1930s, and nobody knows why they bend.

claims.title: Cryptids
claims.standfirst: Cryptozoology has one legitimate test — produce the animal — and one recurring problem: the most famous photograph in the field was confessed to be a toy submarine.

facts.Key survey: Loch Ness eDNA, University of Otago, 2019
facts.What would settle it: A type specimen or diagnostic DNA

claims.title: Crypto AG
claims.standfirst: A Swiss company sold encryption machines to governments around the world for decades. The CIA and the German BND owned it, and the machines were compromised by design.

claims.title: The Crystal Palaces
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Crystal Palace was a glass and iron building of unprecedented scale, and the idea of a 'crystal palace' became a utopian image. It has been read as evidence of lost technology rather than of Victorian engineering.

facts.Fringe reading: A memory of ancient glass technology

claims.title: The Crystal Skulls
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A dozen quartz skulls were said to be pre-Columbian, and one was said to be the work of aliens or Atlanteans. Microscopy found nineteenth-century lapidary tools on every one that has been examined.

facts.Known skulls: About a dozen large quartz examples

claims.title: Cunningham's Law
claims.standfirst: The fastest way to get the right answer online is to post the wrong one. It is a joke about correction culture, and it is accurate often enough to be useful.

facts.Claim: Posting a wrong answer gets faster corrections

claims.title: Curses
claims.standfirst: One curse has been checked with epidemiology, one was dismantled in a courtroom, and one was invented by a newspaper in 1908. All three are still going.

facts.Amityville: Filed as hoax by the SPR

claims.title: The Cyclops and Elephant Skulls
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A suggestion that the Cyclops story came from fossil elephant skulls, whose nasal opening looks like a single eye socket.

claims.title: Damascus Steel
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Blades with a watery pattern, made from crucible steel imported from India, and famous for sharpness. The technique was lost in the eighteenth century, and the nanoscale explanation is contested.

facts.Source steel: Wootz, from India and Sri Lanka
facts.Pattern: Carbide banding from slow cooling and forging

claims.title: The Dancing Plague of 1518
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: In Strasbourg, hundreds of people danced for days without stopping, and some died. The two leading explanations are ergot poisoning and mass psychogenic illness.

facts.Response: Musicians and a stage — dance it out

claims.title: DAOs as Autonomous Firms
claims.standfirst: Organisations run by code and token votes rather than managers. They exist, they hold real money, and their governance has produced both experiments and failures.

claims.title: Dark Flow
claims.standfirst: A 2008 analysis reported that galaxy clusters are all drifting toward a patch of sky beyond the observable universe. If true it would break the assumption that the universe looks the same in every direction. Later data did not confirm it.

facts.Claim: Bulk flow of clusters toward a preferred direction
facts.Reanalysis: Planck and later catalogues: not confirmed

claims.title: The Dark Forest
claims.label_text: A fiction premise, taken as a warning
claims.standfirst: The universe is a dark forest full of armed hunters. Make a sound, and something finds you. It is the most chilling answer to “where is everybody?” — and it was written as a novel.

claims.title: Dark Matter
claims.standfirst: The case that something invisible holds galaxies together is overwhelming. The case for any particular particle is not — and that gap is where the field currently lives.

claims.title: Dark Photons
claims.standfirst: A hypothetical particle that would interact weakly with ordinary matter, proposed as a bridge to a dark sector.

claims.title: Darth Jar Jar
claims.standfirst: A fan theory that Jar Jar Binks was secretly a Sith lord, whose clownish behaviour was a cover. It is inventive, it is argued from staging and dialogue, and its authors know it is fiction.

facts.Claim: Jar Jar was a Sith lord in disguise
facts.Filmmakers: Describe the character as comic relief

claims.title: The Data Wall
claims.standfirst: The claim that training data is running out. The estimate depends on what counts as data.

claims.title: Dating-App Elo Gating
claims.standfirst: The claim that dating apps score users and show them only to people of similar scores. One app did use an Elo-style system, and said it stopped.

facts.Confirmed: Tinder used an Elo-style system early on

claims.title: D. B. Cooper
claims.standfirst: A man hijacked a passenger jet, took $200,000, and jumped into the night over the Pacific Northwest. He was never found, and the case is the only unsolved hijacking in US history.

claims.title: The D.C. Street Grid
claims.standfirst: Washington's diagonal avenues are said to form a pentagram, a Masonic symbol and a satanic layout. They are baroque city planning, and the geometry does not work.

claims.title: De-Extinction
claims.standfirst: Bringing back the mammoth, the thylacine or the passenger pigeon. The genetics is progressing, the ecology is harder, and no de-extincted animal exists yet.

facts.Method: Ancient DNA plus gene editing of a living relative
facts.Achieved: Gene edits in cells; no animals
facts.Closest success: Cloned ferret from frozen tissue — conservation, not de-extinction

claims.title: Dead Hand
claims.standfirst: A Soviet system designed to launch retaliation if the command authority were destroyed — a doomsday machine that actually exists, and is semi-automatic rather than automatic.

claims.title: The Dead Internet Theory
claims.label_text: Half-true, and the true half is worse
claims.standfirst: The claim: most of the internet is no longer people. The data does not support the total version — and the partial version is genuinely unsettling.

claims.title: Dead-Mall Anemoia
claims.standfirst: Nostalgia for places and times the person never knew, spread through images of empty shopping centres.

claims.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Manuscripts hidden in caves near Qumran, including the oldest surviving copies of biblical texts. They were found by Bedouin shepherds.

claims.title: Deadpool's Fourth Wall
claims.standfirst: The character talks to the reader. The convention is documented; the 'proof' it gives about the character's world is not.

claims.title: Dear David
claims.standfirst: A Twitter thread about a ghost in an apartment, told in real time with drawings and photographs. It was a performance, and it was very good.

claims.title: The Deep Biosphere's Extent
claims.standfirst: Microbes live in rock kilometres below the surface, and they may account for a large fraction of the planet's biomass. How much, and how active, is argued.

claims.title: Deep Web & Dark Web
claims.standfirst: Ninety per cent of the web is “deep” in the most boring possible sense: it is behind a login, a paywall, or a search box. The dark web is a small encrypted subset of that, and it is not a place.

facts.Deep web: ~90% of the web; unindexed, mostly ordinary
facts.Dark web: Deliberately concealed; needs Tor or I2P

claims.title: Deepfake Detection
claims.standfirst: Tools to spot synthetic media, and the arms race against them. Detection works sometimes.

claims.title: Deepwater Horizon Cement
claims.standfirst: A well blowout that killed eleven people and spilled millions of barrels. The cement job and the decisions around it are documented.

claims.title: Déjà Rêvé
claims.standfirst: The sense that this moment was dreamed before. It is distinct from déjà vu, it is common, and the tempting explanation — that the dream predicted the event — is the one the evidence does not support.

facts.Experience: A present moment felt to have been dreamed
facts.Distinct from: Déjà vu, which has no dream attribution
facts.Likely mechanism: Memory reconstruction at the moment of the event

claims.title: Déjà Vu
claims.standfirst: The feeling that this has happened before, with no memory of when. Most people have it, nobody has a settled explanation, and the one thing it is not is evidence of a previous life.

claims.title: The Delphic Ethylene
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A theory that the oracle at Delphi was inspired by ethylene gas rising from a fault. The geology is real; the effect is argued.

claims.title: Democratic Peace
claims.standfirst: Kant predicted it in 1795. Statistical work from the 1960s found it. Democracies fight plenty of wars — just not, on the whole, each other — and the explanation matters enormously for policy.

facts.Claim: Dyadic: democracies rarely fight each other
facts.Not claimed: That democracies are peaceful in general

claims.title: Democritus and Atoms
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A Greek philosopher argued that matter consists of indivisible particles. He had no evidence, and he was right.

claims.title: The Dendera Light
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A relief at Dendera shows a bulb-shaped object with a snake inside it. The claim that it depicts an electric lamp ignores the rest of the scene, which explains it.

facts.Missing: Glass, electrodes, wires, a power source

claims.title: Denisovan Inheritance
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A hominin known from a finger bone, whose genes are in living people from Tibet to Melanesia.

claims.title: Derinkuyu
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: An underground city in Cappadocia with rooms, stables, a church and ventilation shafts, deep enough for thousands of people.

claims.title: Detox Foot Pads
claims.standfirst: Patches that turn brown overnight and are said to draw out toxins. The colour is oxidation.

claims.title: The Devil's Footprints
claims.standfirst: Hoof-like prints appeared across Devon overnight, in a line, over walls and roofs. The snow was real; the explanation is still argued.

claims.title: Die Glocke
claims.standfirst: A supposed Nazi secret weapon called 'the Bell': a bell-shaped device said to use exotic physics. It appears in a 2000 book, and there is no contemporary document.

facts.Claimed: A bell-shaped device with exotic effects
facts.Site: Lower Silesia; a mine cooling tower

claims.title: Dieselgate
claims.standfirst: Volkswagen fitted cars with software that detected emissions tests and switched on full pollution control only when being tested. On the road, the cars emitted many times the limit.

facts.Emissions: Up to 40× the limit on the road
facts.Executives: Charged; two imprisoned in the US

claims.title: Dighton Rock
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A boulder covered in carvings, attributed to Phoenicians, Norse, Portuguese and Indigenous peoples.

claims.title: Digital-Twin Predictive Policing
claims.standfirst: The claim that cities will be policed through real-time simulations of their populations. The components exist; the system does not.

claims.title: The Dinosaur Extinction
claims.standfirst: An asteroid hit the Yucatán 66 million years ago and three quarters of species died. The argument about whether the impact or the Deccan volcanoes did it is now mostly an argument about timing, and the timing has been measured.

facts.Key marker: Worldwide iridium anomaly and ejecta layer

claims.title: Dinosaur Metabolism
claims.standfirst: Were the dinosaurs warm-blooded? Bone growth, isotopes and the nasal anatomy point in different directions, and the answer may be neither.

claims.title: Unresolved Disappearances
claims.standfirst: A ship found sailing itself, a pilot who vanished over an ocean, five children who left no remains. These are the cases where the evidence ran out rather than pointed somewhere.

facts.Label: Still open
facts.Cases here: Six detailed, one class of small cases

claims.title: The Default Mode Network and Ego Death
claims.standfirst: Psychedelics reduce activity in the brain network associated with self-referential thought, and people report the dissolution of the self. The correlation is documented; the interpretation is not.

claims.title: The Dungeons & Dragons Panic
claims.standfirst: A game blamed for suicides and Satanism. The evidence was never there, and the panic is documented.

claims.title: Doggerland
claims.standfirst: A landmass in the southern North Sea, drowned between about 8,000 and 7,000 years ago. Trawlers have brought up bones and tools for a century.

claims.title: The Dogon and Sirius B
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Dogon of Mali are said to have known that Sirius has a tiny, dense companion with a fifty-year orbit, centuries before telescopes could see it. The fieldwork behind the claim is the problem.

facts.Claim: Knowledge of Sirius B's orbit and density
facts.Timing problem: Sirius B's properties known in print first

claims.title: Dogū as Astronauts
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Clay figurines from Jōmon Japan have goggle-like eyes and patterned bodies. They were read as space suits. They are stylised figures, mostly female, and many were deliberately broken.

claims.title: Domestication Syndrome
claims.standfirst: Domesticated animals share a set of traits — floppy ears, patchy coats, smaller brains — and the explanation is argued.

facts.Traits: Floppy ears; patchy coats; smaller brains

claims.title: Doofenshmirtz Is Phineas's Father
claims.standfirst: A theory that the cartoon villain is the boys' father. It is an interpretation, and the show has not confirmed it.

claims.title: The Doomsday Argument
claims.standfirst: You were born somewhere in the human sequence, not at a special point in it. Apply that assumption and the numbers say the species probably ends within a few thousand years. The argument turns entirely on whether the assumption is legitimate.

claims.title: The Door to Hell
claims.standfirst: A gas crater in Turkmenistan has been burning since 1971, and it looks like an entrance to the underworld. It is a collapsed gas cavity, set alight to burn off the gas.

claims.title: The Dorchester Pot
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A brass vessel was found in rock in 1852 and dated to the deep past. It is a nineteenth-century ornament, and the 'rock' is a conglomerate that formed around it.

claims.title: The Dragonborn Is Shor
claims.standfirst: A theory about the player character's identity in a game's mythology. It is an interpretation of a fiction.

claims.title: Dragons from Fossils
claims.standfirst: The suggestion that dragon myths around the world grew from fossil bones. The bones are everywhere; the stories differ.

claims.title: Dragons & Dinosaurs
claims.standfirst: Every culture on Earth independently invented a giant reptile. In 2013, a team tried to work out whether they did it independently at all.

claims.title: The Dropa Stones
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Stone discs with spiral grooves, said to have been found in a Chinese cave with the remains of a dwarf people, and said to record an alien crash. No museum has them and no archaeologist saw them.

claims.title: The Dulce Base
claims.standfirst: A claimed secret underground facility beneath New Mexico, housing aliens and joint projects. The claims rest on one man's testimony.

claims.title: Dunbar's Number
claims.standfirst: Dunbar plotted neocortex size against group size across primates and extrapolated to humans: about 150 stable relationships. Armies, firms and villages seemed to fit. Then the statistics were redone.

facts.Online: Layer structure persists; friend counts do not

claims.title: Dune as Anti-Messiah
claims.standfirst: Frank Herbert wrote Dune as a warning about charismatic leaders and the danger of following them. The films and the fandom have often read it as a hero story.

facts.Contested: How clear the first book is

claims.title: Dunning–Kruger
claims.standfirst: Low performers overestimate their ability. The effect is real and the popular version — a graph with a peak of confidence on a mountain of stupidity — is not what the paper showed.

facts.Finding: Low performers overestimate their percentile rank
facts.Explanation offered: Metacognitive: skill is needed to judge skill
facts.Statistical caveat: Much of the pattern is regression to the mean
facts.Popular version: The 'Mount Stupid' curve — not in the data

claims.title: The Dursleys and a Horcrux
claims.standfirst: A theory that the Dursleys' cruelty is explained by Harry being a Horcrux. The books give the Horcrux explanation for other effects, and not for this.

facts.Problem: The effect would have to be selective

claims.title: Dutch Disease
claims.standfirst: A resource boom that hollows out the rest of the economy by raising the currency.

claims.title: Dwarka
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Ruins have been found under the sea off Gujarat, and they are real. The claim that they are the 32,000-year-old city of Krishna is not supported by their dating.

claims.title: Dyatlov Pass
claims.standfirst: Nine experienced ski hikers cut their way out of a tent in the night and died in the snow. Sixty years later, two physicists modelled the snow and closed most of the gap.

claims.title: Dyson Spheres
claims.standfirst: A civilisation that captured all its star's light would be visible from far away, as an excess of infrared and a deficit of visible light. Astronomers have looked, and found candidates that turned out to be dust.

claims.title: Dyson Swarms
claims.standfirst: A solid shell around a star is gravitationally impossible. A swarm of collectors is not, and the difference matters: the swarm is the version astronomers actually search for.

claims.title: The Early Geodynamo
claims.standfirst: The Earth's magnetic field is generated by a dynamo in the core, and it was running more than three billion years ago. How, with a hotter core, is the problem.

facts.Problem: A hot core resists thermal convection

claims.title: Earthquake Prediction
claims.standfirst: Nobody can say where and when a large earthquake will happen. A great deal of money and a long list of methods have gone into trying, and the failures are more instructive than the successes.

facts.What works: Aftershock statistics, hazard maps, early warning
facts.Haicheng / Tangshan: 1975 warned, 1976 not — the same country, one year apart

claims.title: The East Palestine Burn
claims.standfirst: A derailment, then a controlled burn of vinyl chloride that sent a plume over the town. Both are documented.

claims.title: The Easterlin Paradox
claims.standfirst: Richer countries are happier; richer people within them are happier; but growth over time does not raise happiness much.

facts.Author: Richard Easterlin, 1974
facts.Finding: Little rise in happiness with growth

claims.title: Echo Chambers
claims.standfirst: The theory is intuitive: recommendation systems show you what you already agree with, and you drift outward. The experiments that changed people's feeds found the drift was smaller than expected — and not always in the predicted direction.

facts.Attitude effect: Small or absent in the trial windows

claims.title: Eden in Mesopotamia
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that the Genesis garden can be located by its rivers. The text names four rivers; two cannot be identified.

claims.title: Eden in Missouri
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that the Garden of Eden was in Missouri, with a stone altar to prove it. The stone is real; the garden is not.

claims.title: The Ediacaran Organisms
claims.standfirst: For decades, the Ediacaran fossils were a taxonomic orphanage: too big to be microbes, too weird to be animals. Molecular evidence has now placed some of them, without settling the group.

claims.title: The Efficiency Wage
claims.standfirst: Paying above the market rate can raise productivity. The theory is documented; the size is argued.

claims.title: The Egg
claims.standfirst: Every person who has ever lived is you, living every life in turn. It is a short story by the man who wrote The Martian — and the internet turned it into a theory.

facts.Author: Andy Weir, 2009
facts.Testable: No — and it does not claim to be

claims.title: Eggs and Cholesterol
claims.standfirst: Dietary cholesterol was said to raise blood cholesterol and heart risk. The advice has been revised, and the debate continues.

claims.title: Ego's Childhood Cottage
claims.standfirst: A theory that a planet-sized character's memories are fabrications. It is an interpretation of a film.

claims.title: Ego Depletion
claims.standfirst: For fifteen years, 'willpower is a finite resource like a battery' was textbook psychology, complete with the advice to drink sugar water. Then the replications came back near zero.

claims.title: Egyptian Surgery
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A papyrus describes forty-eight surgical cases with examinations, diagnoses and treatments, including the brain.

claims.title: The Ekpyrotic Universe
claims.standfirst: A model in which the Big Bang is the collision of two branes in a higher-dimensional space. It replaces inflation with a collision, and the two make different predictions.

claims.title: El Dorado
claims.standfirst: The legend of a city of gold began as a ritual: a Muisca chief covered in gold dust, offering at a lake. Expeditions killed thousands looking for a place that was never there.

facts.Meaning: 'The gilded one' — a person, not a place

claims.title: The Eleusinian Kykeon
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A theory that the drink at the Eleusinian mysteries contained a psychedelic fungus. The rite is documented; the drug is not.

claims.title: The Elisa Lam Tapes
claims.standfirst: A student died in a Los Angeles hotel in 2013, and the elevator footage of her last hours became one of the internet's most analysed videos. The official finding is an accidental drowning; the theories have not stopped.

facts.Setting: A hotel with a documented safety record

claims.title: Elsagate
claims.standfirst: Children's videos on YouTube were infiltrated by content with inappropriate themes, surfaced by recommendation. The scandal was real, the platform response was documented, and the underlying problem has not gone away.

claims.title: Embodied Cognition
claims.standfirst: The claim that thinking is shaped by having a body — that concepts are grounded in sensorimotor experience. It is well supported in some domains and over-claimed in others.

facts.Over-claim: The body thinks; the brain is not central

claims.title: Emergent Abilities
claims.standfirst: Big models were said to suddenly acquire skills. The suddenness turned out to be the metric's fault.

claims.title: Emergent Gravity
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The proposal that gravity is not fundamental but arises from deeper physics, as temperature arises from atoms.

claims.title: Enron and California
claims.standfirst: California's electricity market was deregulated, and traders found ways to make money by creating scarcity. The state had rolling blackouts, and Enron collapsed.

claims.title: Enshittification
claims.standfirst: First the platform is good to you, then it is good to its business customers, then it is good to nobody but its shareholders. The pattern is real; the law is not.

facts.Evidence: FTC v. Amazon (2023); app-store antitrust cases
facts.Weakness: Hard to falsify; a moral frame as well as a model

claims.title: Entropic Gravity
claims.standfirst: The proposal that gravity is not a fundamental force but an emergent consequence of entropy. It is elegant, it made a testable prediction, and the test disagreed.

claims.title: Epigenetic Inheritance of Trauma
claims.standfirst: The claim that trauma leaves chemical marks on DNA that pass to children and grandchildren. The human studies are small and confounded; the mechanism is real in animals and unproven in people.

claims.title: ER = EPR
claims.standfirst: The proposal that wormholes and quantum entanglement are the same phenomenon, described by two different theories. It is elegant, influential and unproved.

facts.Claim: Wormholes and entanglement are the same

claims.title: Eratosthenes Measured the Earth
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A librarian in Alexandria calculated the circumference of the Earth from a shadow and a distance, and got within a few per cent. The method is documented.

claims.title: Erratas and the KFC Link
claims.standfirst: A set of videos with hidden codes that pointed, apparently, at a fast-food chain. The codes are real; the meaning is not settled.

claims.title: Eskimo Snow Words
claims.standfirst: The claim that Inuit languages have hundreds of words for snow. The number was invented by a populariser and has been repeated ever since.

claims.title: E.T. and Star Wars
claims.standfirst: A cameo put E.T.'s species in the Star Wars senate, and a fan theory built a shared universe on it. The cameo is real; the universe is a joke.

claims.title: The Etruscans
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The civilisation that taught Rome its rituals, and whose language is still only partly read. Their origin was argued for centuries and settled by DNA.

claims.title: The First Eukaryote
claims.standfirst: Every animal, plant and fungus descends from a cell that swallowed a bacterium and kept it. The swallowing is certain; the swallow-er is not.

facts.Open: Identity of the host; timing; one event or many

claims.title: Europa's Ocean
claims.standfirst: Beneath fifteen kilometres of ice, Europa has more liquid water than all of Earth's oceans. Whether anything lives in it is unknown, and a spacecraft is on its way to look.

facts.Evidence: Induced magnetic field; young fractured surface

claims.title: Evangelion's Loop
claims.standfirst: A theory that the series repeats, with the same events happening again and again. The show's ending is strange enough to support several readings.

claims.title: The Evil Farming Game
claims.standfirst: A remembered game about a farmer with a dark secret, searched for and never found. The likely answer is a memory blend.

claims.title: Evil Morty's Curve
claims.standfirst: The theory that the show's plot is driven by a statistical curve of Mortys. It is a joke about narrative and it is treated as one.

claims.title: Evolutionary Modularity
claims.standfirst: The claim that the mind is a collection of specialised modules shaped by Pleistocene selection. It is productive and contested, and the evidence for specific modules is thinner than the framework.

claims.title: Expanding Earth
claims.standfirst: The claim that the Earth has grown over time, with the continents fitting together on a smaller globe. Plate tectonics explains the same fit without the growth.

claims.title: The Extended Synthesis
claims.standfirst: The proposal that evolutionary theory needs more than the modern synthesis: development, plasticity, inheritance beyond genes.

claims.title: Eyewitness Identification
claims.standfirst: The most persuasive evidence in a courtroom and one of the least reliable, as DNA exonerations showed.

claims.title: Ezekiel's Wheel
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A vision of wheels within wheels, read by some as a description of a spacecraft. The text is a prophetic vision.

claims.title: The Face on Mars
claims.standfirst: A mesa in the Cydonia region looked like a face at Viking resolution. Higher-resolution images, taken twenty-two years later, show a mesa. The interesting part is why the first image looked the way it did.

facts.Mechanism: Pareidolia plus low resolution and low sun
facts.Concealment claim: No — the other frames were released

claims.title: Facebook's Teen Research
claims.standfirst: Internal studies found harms to teenage users, and the company's own researchers said so. The documents were disclosed by a whistleblower.

claims.title: Facial Feedback
claims.standfirst: Holding a pen in your teeth makes cartoons funnier, according to a 1988 study. A 17-lab replication failed to find it, and the argument since has been about what that means.

facts.Method: Pen in the teeth versus the lips

claims.title: False Confessions
claims.standfirst: People confess to crimes they did not commit, and the reasons are documented.

claims.title: Operation Fast and Furious
claims.standfirst: US agents allowed firearms to be trafficked into Mexico in order to trace them, and lost track of most of them. Two were found at the scene of a Border Patrol agent's killing.

claims.title: Fast & Furious Mutation
claims.standfirst: A joke that the series' characters have become superheroes, and that the films record a mutation. It is a description of escalation, not a plot.

claims.title: Fast Radio Bursts
claims.standfirst: Millisecond flashes of radio energy from other galaxies, first dismissed as a microwave oven and now observed in their thousands. The phenomenon is documented; the source of most of them is still open.

facts.Signature: Millisecond pulse with a large dispersion measure
facts.Still open: The engine of the brightest bursts

claims.title: The FBI and Martin Luther King
claims.standfirst: The FBI wiretapped King, bugged his hotel rooms, and sent him an anonymous letter urging suicide. The campaign is documented in the Bureau's own files.

claims.title: The FDA–Purdue Door
claims.standfirst: A drug label change negotiated between a regulator and the company, and the revolving door around it.

claims.title: The Feejee Mermaid
claims.theme: Anomalies, fringe science and the unexplained
claims.standfirst: A mermaid exhibited by P. T. Barnum was a monkey's torso sewn to a fish's tail. It made money, started a genre, and is still in a museum drawer with the stitching visible.

facts.Exhibited: New York, 1842, by P. T. Barnum
facts.Construction: Monkey torso, fish tail, joined and dried
facts.Modern descendant: Every exhibit that invites disbelief as proof

claims.title: Fibre Analysis
claims.standfirst: Fibres transfer between people and places. The transfer is real; the identification is weaker than it sounds.

claims.title: FIFA Bribes
claims.standfirst: Senior football officials were indicted in the United States for racketeering and bribery over media and marketing rights. The president resigned.

claims.title: Fingerprint Individuality
claims.standfirst: Fingerprints are unique in practice, and examiners' claims of certainty are a separate matter.

claims.title: The Firewall Paradox
claims.standfirst: In 2012 four physicists showed that a falling observer at a black-hole horizon cannot both see empty space and preserve quantum information. The field has been arguing about which assumption to give up ever since.

facts.Conflict: Monogamy of entanglement at the horizon

claims.title: The Five-Second Rule
