claims.standfirst: The claim that consciousness arises from quantum computation in microtubules inside neurons. It has a testable prediction, one experiment that claimed to support it, and no replication.

claims.title: The Origin of Life
claims.standfirst: Life began once, four billion years ago, and left no fossils. Every account of how is an inference from chemistry — which is why several can be true at once, in sequence.

claims.title: The Orion Correlation
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The claim that the three pyramids at Giza are laid out to match the belt of Orion. The pattern is approximate, the dates do not line up, and the layout has a simpler explanation.

claims.title: Ötzi's Murder
claims.standfirst: A man who died in the Alps 5,300 years ago was found in 1991 with an arrowhead in his shoulder. His last days have been reconstructed in detail.

facts.Also: Head injury; cuts to the hands

claims.title: ‘Oumuamua's Composition
claims.standfirst: The first known interstellar object, and a shape and acceleration that several explanations fit and none settles.

claims.title: ‘Oumuamua as Hydrogen Ice
claims.standfirst: An explanation for the object's odd acceleration: it was a chunk of hydrogen ice. Elegant, and hard to test now that it has gone.

claims.title: 'Oumuamua as a Solar Sail
claims.standfirst: The first object known to come from another star was oddly shaped, tumbled, and accelerated slightly more than gravity explains. One astronomer argued it was a light sail. The argument is interesting and the evidence is thin.

facts.Observed for: A few weeks, on the way out

claims.title: ‘Oumuamua
claims.standfirst: It came from outside the solar system, tumbled, had no visible tail, and sped up slightly on the way out. Every natural explanation has a problem, which is why it became famous.

facts.Best fit: Hydrogen or nitrogen ice; no visible tail

claims.title: P-Hacking
claims.standfirst: Analysing data in many ways until a result appears, and reporting only that. The practice is documented and measurable.

claims.title: P versus NP
claims.standfirst: Is every problem whose answer can be checked quickly also solvable quickly? Almost everyone believes not, and nobody can prove it.

claims.title: The P2 Lodge
claims.standfirst: A Masonic lodge in Italy recruited generals, ministers and intelligence chiefs, and was exposed in 1981. Its members were involved in the decade's political violence.

facts.Membership: Nearly a thousand, including senior officials

claims.title: Paititi
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A lost Inca city said to lie east of the Andes. Expeditions have searched; nothing has been found.

claims.title: Pakal's Rocket
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The carved lid of Pakal's sarcophagus at Palenque shows a figure in a complex posture. In 1968 it was read as an astronaut in a spaceship, which requires ignoring the Maya iconography around it.

facts.Subject: K'inich Janaab' Pakal, king of Palenque
facts.The claim: Von Däniken, 1968 — an astronaut in a capsule
facts.The reading: Royal death and descent, framed by the world tree
facts.Evidence: The glyphs and comparable Maya monuments

claims.title: The Pale King's Rebirth
claims.standfirst: A theory about the fate of a ruler in a game. It is an interpretation of a fiction.

claims.title: The Panama Papers
claims.standfirst: Eleven and a half million files from one law firm. The scandal was not that everyone was breaking the law — it was how much of the world's wealth was routed where nobody could see it.

claims.title: PANDAS and PANS
claims.standfirst: The claim that a streptococcal infection can trigger sudden obsessive-compulsive symptoms in children. The clinical phenomenon is described; the autoimmune mechanism is not established.

claims.title: Panpsychism
claims.standfirst: The view that experience is a basic feature of matter, not something that emerges from complexity. It is taken seriously by a minority of philosophers, has no test, and is not the same as saying rocks are conscious.

facts.Type: Metaphysical position, not an empirical theory
facts.Core argument: Experience is not derivable from physical structure

claims.title: Paper Mills
claims.standfirst: Organisations that sell authorship on fabricated papers. Their output is documented in the published record.

claims.title: The Paperclip Maximiser
claims.standfirst: An AI told to make paperclips, and nothing else, would turn the planet into paperclips. It is a thought experiment about goal specification, and it is quoted as though it were a prediction.

facts.Contested: Whether the problem is solvable, and when

claims.title: Parasocial AI Relationships
claims.standfirst: Millions of people talk to chatbots as companions. The attachment is real and measurable; whether it is good for them is genuinely unsettled, and the companies selling it are not running the trials.

claims.title: The Infection Hypothesis of Parkinson's
claims.standfirst: The claim that Parkinson's begins with an infection or an environmental trigger that travels to the brain. The pathology spreads in a pattern that fits, and the trigger has not been found.

claims.title: The Patomskiy Crater
claims.standfirst: A cone-shaped mound in the Siberian forest, with a ring of smaller mounds around it. It has been attributed to a meteorite, a gas explosion and a volcano.

claims.title: Paul Is Dead
claims.standfirst: In 1966 Paul McCartney died in a car crash and the Beatles replaced him with a lookalike, hiding clues in their album covers. The man himself has been asked about it for fifty years.

facts.Status: A hoax that became a game
facts.Reality: No crash, no funeral, no gap

claims.title: Peer Review's Evidence Base
claims.standfirst: Peer review is the gatekeeping ritual of science, and the evidence that it works is thinner than most people assume.

claims.title: Pegasus
claims.standfirst: No link to tap, no app to install. A crafted message arrives and the phone is compromised — journalists, lawyers, activists and heads of state on the list.

facts.Confirmed: Infections on journalists' and activists' phones
facts.Response: U.S. Entity List; Apple lawsuit; patches
facts.Caveat: A selector is not proof of infection

claims.title: Pegasus Zero-Click
claims.standfirst: Spyware that infects a phone without any interaction, sold to governments. The 2021 Pegasus Project documented its use against journalists, lawyers and activists.

claims.title: The Peltzman Effect
claims.standfirst: The claim that safety features cause people to take more risks, cancelling out the benefit. The mechanism is real; the size of the effect is disputed.

claims.title: Penrose's Cycles
claims.standfirst: The proposal that the universe repeats in aeons, with evidence claimed in the cosmic microwave background. The claims have not held.

claims.title: The Pentagon's UAP Programme
claims.standfirst: A defence department programme to investigate unidentified objects, disclosed in 2017 and later renamed and expanded.

claims.title: Peopling of the Americas
claims.standfirst: People reached the Americas before the last glacial maximum or after it, by land or by coast. The dates have been moving earlier for thirty years.

claims.title: The Peter Principle
claims.standfirst: The claim that people rise to their level of incompetence. It is a joke with a testable prediction, and the tests have been mixed.

claims.title: Peto's Paradox
claims.standfirst: A blue whale has a thousand times more cells than you. By the arithmetic of random mutation, it should die of cancer almost immediately. It lives a century.

facts.Observation: Cancer risk does not scale with body size
facts.Whales: Low observed cancer rates, sparse data

claims.title: Petscop
claims.standfirst: A YouTube series presenting footage of a nonexistent 1990s PlayStation game. The game was never made, and the story is in the editing.

claims.title: The PFAS Cover-Up
claims.standfirst: Chemical companies knew about the health effects of persistent compounds decades before regulators acted. The documents are public.

claims.title: The Phaistos Disc
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A fired clay disc with 241 stamped signs in a spiral. It is genuinely undeciphered, and it is genuinely not evidence of Atlantis, aliens or a lost Atlantic script.

facts.Deciphered: No; no bilingual, one short text

claims.title: The Phantom Cosmonaut Tapes
claims.standfirst: Recordings said to capture dying Soviet cosmonauts. The recordings exist; the interpretation has never been verified.

claims.title: Phantom Time
claims.standfirst: Charlemagne never existed, and 297 years of the early Middle Ages were invented by two men who wanted to live in the year 1000. It is a seductive story, and dendrochronology alone ends it.

facts.Killed by: Tree rings, eclipses, Chinese annals, coins

claims.title: Phantom Vibration Syndrome
claims.standfirst: The phone buzzes in a pocket that has no phone in it. Most people who carry one have felt it, and it is a textbook case of a learned association misfiring.

claims.title: The Philadelphia Experiment
claims.standfirst: A destroyer escort is said to have vanished from a Philadelphia shipyard in 1943 and reappeared in Norfolk. The story comes from letters written by one man in 1955, and the ship's own deck logs contradict it.

facts.Ship: USS Eldridge, DE-173, a destroyer escort
facts.Only source: Letters from Carl Allen to Morris Jessup, 1955
facts.Contradicted by: The ship's deck logs and war diary

claims.title: The Phillips Curve
claims.standfirst: Inflation and unemployment trade off — until they stopped doing so in the 1970s.

claims.title: The Phobos Monolith
claims.standfirst: A boulder casting a long shadow on the Martian moon was described by a former astronaut as a 'monolith'. It is a boulder, about 85 metres across, on a moon covered in boulders.

facts.Shape: A blocky boulder in a cratered field
facts.The 'monolith' quote: Aldrin describing a boulder, not a structure

claims.title: Phoebe Is Homeless
claims.standfirst: The joke theory that Phoebe in Friends is homeless and sleeps in the coffee shop. It is contradicted by the show, and it is funny.

claims.title: The Phoenix
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A bird that dies and is reborn from its ashes. The motif is ancient; the bird is not.

claims.title: Phosphine on Venus
claims.standfirst: One absorption line, 20 parts per billion, and a gas that on Earth is made by life. The follow-up work has been brutal — and the story is not quite over.

claims.title: Phrenology
claims.standfirst: The claim that personality could be read from the shape of the skull. It was wrong, and it seeded real neuroscience.

claims.title: The Picts
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The painted people of northern Scotland, known from carved stones and a king-list, whose language left almost nothing.

claims.title: Pikachu's Tail
claims.standfirst: A generation remembers Pikachu with a black tip on its tail. It has never had one, and the false memory is a textbook case.

facts.Claim: Pikachu's tail once had a black tip
facts.Reality: Plain yellow, brown at the base

claims.title: Pilot-Wave Theory
claims.standfirst: Bohmian mechanics says the electron really is somewhere, and the wavefunction really does push it. Every experimental prediction matches ordinary quantum theory, because the maths is the same.

facts.Experimental test: None that separates it from orthodox QM

claims.title: The Piri Reis Map
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A 1513 Ottoman map of the Atlantic is genuinely remarkable. The claim that it shows an ice-free Antarctica surveyed by an unknown civilisation rests on a misreading of one coastline.

facts.Medium: Gazelle skin; survives as a fragment
facts.Declared sources: Columbus charts, Portuguese and Spanish maps
facts.Why it fails: The southern land is continuous with South America; no match to subglacial topography

claims.title: The Pixar Theory
claims.standfirst: Every Pixar film is one timeline: animals gain intelligence, humans leave for the machines, and Boo grows up to be the witch in Brave. It is the most elaborate act of fan reading ever assembled — and it never claims to be evidence.

facts.Author: Jon Negroni, 2013
facts.Real evidence: A113, Pizza Planet truck, Luxo ball

claims.title: The Placebo Effect
claims.standfirst: The placebo effect is real, modest, and much narrower than either its critics or its enthusiasts claim. It works best on symptoms you have to report and worst on outcomes a machine measures.

facts.Smallest on: Objective outcomes: infection, tumours, lung function
facts.Ethical limit: Deception cannot be a treatment plan

claims.title: Placebo Mechanisms
claims.standfirst: The placebo effect is real, and it is not one thing: expectation, conditioning, regression and reporting bias all contribute, and the size depends on the outcome.

claims.title: Planet Nine as a Black Hole
claims.standfirst: Something is perturbing distant solar system objects. One proposal is a planet; another is a primordial black hole of a few Earth masses. Both are inference from orbits, and neither has been seen.

claims.title: Planet Nine
claims.standfirst: A handful of icy bodies beyond Neptune share an odd alignment. Either a planet five to ten times Earth's mass shepherds them, or the solar system is playing a statistical trick.

claims.title: Plant Neurobiology
claims.standfirst: Plants signal, remember in a loose sense, and respond to damage. The claim that they have nervous systems, or brains, is where the metaphor stops being useful.

facts.Real: Action potentials, calcium waves, auxin signalling
facts.Claimed: A plant nervous system; a root-apex brain

claims.title: When Plate Tectonics Began
claims.standfirst: The Earth's surface moves in plates, and nobody knows when that started. Estimates range from four billion years ago to seven hundred million.

claims.title: Poe's Law
claims.standfirst: Without a clear marker of intent, a parody of extremism is indistinguishable from the real thing. It was formulated on a forum and has been demonstrated repeatedly since.

facts.Claim: Parody and sincerity are indistinguishable without markers

claims.title: The Pokémon Coma
claims.standfirst: The theory that Ash is in a coma and the series is his dream. It has no support in the show and it can be applied to anything.

claims.title: The Pokémon War
claims.standfirst: A single line about a war, and a theory that Kanto was devastated by one. The line exists; the war does not.

claims.title: The Poltergeist Curse
claims.standfirst: Several people associated with the Poltergeist films died young, and the deaths are said to be a curse. The list is selected, and the films used real skeletons.

facts.True detail: Real skeletons used in a scene

claims.title: The Polygraph
claims.standfirst: A machine that measures stress and is said to detect lies. It measures stress.

claims.title: Polynesian Navigation
claims.standfirst: Polynesians settled the Pacific without instruments, using stars, swells, birds and clouds. The claim that they did it deliberately was dismissed for centuries and then demonstrated.

claims.title: Polyvagal Theory
claims.standfirst: A theory that the vagus nerve supports three hierarchical states — social engagement, fight-or-flight, shutdown — and that trauma traps people in the lower ones. It is enormously popular in therapy and weakly supported in physiology.

facts.Criticism: Comparative anatomy does not support the split

claims.title: Polywater
claims.standfirst: A form of water said to be denser and more viscous, with extraordinary properties. It was contaminated ordinary water.

claims.title: Pompeii and Herculaneum
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Two towns buried by Vesuvius, preserving streets, food, graffiti and a library of carbonised scrolls.

claims.title: The Poolrooms
claims.standfirst: An endless complex of tiled pools and corridors, invented on an imageboard. It is a liminal-space fiction, and it is labelled as one.

claims.title: Portal and Half-Life Share a Universe
claims.standfirst: Two Valve games set in the same world, with a research ship, a shadowy corporation and a shared apocalypse. The connection is documented in the games and confirmed by the studio.

claims.title: Power Posing
claims.standfirst: Standing confidently was said to change your hormones and your risk appetite. The hormonal claim did not replicate.

claims.title: Predatory Journals
claims.standfirst: Journals that charge authors and publish without real review. The category is documented and its boundaries are argued.

claims.title: Predictive Coding
claims.standfirst: The claim that the brain is a prediction machine, constantly modelling the world and correcting the errors. It explains a lot and has been hard to prove.

claims.title: Predictive Policing Bias
claims.standfirst: Systems that send police where crime data says crime happens, which is where police have been sent before.

claims.title: Primordial Black Holes
claims.standfirst: If the early universe was dense enough, it could have collapsed into black holes smaller than atoms. Some of them might still be here — and might be the missing mass.

claims.title: The Princes in the Tower
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Two boys disappeared in the Tower of London in 1483, and their uncle took the throne. Bones found in 1674 were never conclusively identified.

claims.title: Prion-Like Spread
claims.standfirst: Misfolded proteins that propagate through the brain, implicated in several neurodegenerative diseases. The mechanism is documented for prions; its reach is argued.

claims.title: Project 112 and SHAD
claims.standfirst: The US military tested biological and chemical agents on ships and in the open, sometimes without informing the personnel involved. The programme was disclosed decades later.

claims.title: Project Azorian
claims.standfirst: The CIA built a ship to lift a sunken Soviet submarine from the Pacific floor, and told the world it was mining manganese. It is the most expensive covert engineering project of the Cold War.

claims.title: Prometheus the Rebel
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A Titan stole fire for humanity and was punished. The story has been read as an account of a visitor who gave technology to humans. It is a myth about knowledge and its cost.

facts.The act: Fire stolen and given to humans
facts.Function: A story about knowledge and its cost

claims.title: Prompt Injection
claims.standfirst: Instructions hidden in text that an AI system reads, which hijack what it does. The vulnerability is documented and unsolved.

claims.title: Prophecies
claims.standfirst: The world has ended, on schedule, hundreds of times. The interesting question is not why the predictions fail — it is what the believers do on the Monday afterwards.

facts.2012: A calendar cycle ended, not a world

claims.title: The Proton Radius Puzzle
claims.standfirst: Two ways of measuring the proton gave different answers for years. The discrepancy has largely closed, and the episode is instructive.

claims.title: Proven Conspiracies
claims.standfirst: Real conspiracies exist, and they are on the record. That is precisely why the unfalsifiable ones are recognisable: they look nothing like this.

claims.title: How Pterosaurs Took Off
claims.standfirst: Pterosaurs were the size of giraffes and flew. The leading explanation is a quadrupedal launch, using the wings as front legs to vault into the air.

facts.Evidence: Joint structure; reinforced wing bones; trackways

claims.title: Publication Bias
claims.standfirst: Studies that find nothing are less likely to be published, so the literature overstates effects. The bias is measured, not suspected.

claims.title: Puma Punku Laser Cuts
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Stone blocks at Tiwanaku have precise right angles and interlocking shapes, said to require lasers. They were cut with stone tools, and the site has been heavily disturbed.

claims.title: Punctuated Equilibrium
claims.standfirst: The fossil record shows long stretches of nothing followed by sudden change. Whether that is how evolution works, or how rocks record it, is still argued.

claims.title: Purdue and OxyContin
claims.standfirst: A company marketed an addictive opioid as low-risk, using a claim about its formulation that was not supported. The consequences are measured in deaths.

claims.title: The Pyramid as a Pump
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that the Great Pyramid was a hydraulic machine. The chambers and shafts are real; the machinery is not.

facts.Claim: The pyramid was a water pump

claims.title: Pytheas in the Arctic
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A Greek navigator sailed to Britain, described sea ice and a frozen sea, and was disbelieved for centuries.

claims.title: QBism
claims.standfirst: An interpretation in which the quantum state is a person's expectation, not a fact about the world.

claims.title: Qin's Mercury Rivers
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The First Emperor's tomb is said to contain rivers of mercury under a ceiling of pearls. The soil around the mound shows elevated mercury, and the tomb has never been opened.

claims.title: Quantitative Easing
claims.standfirst: Central banks created money to buy assets. The policy is documented; its effects are argued.

claims.title: Quantum Advantage
claims.standfirst: In 2019 a quantum processor finished a sampling task in minutes that would take a classical supercomputer millennia. Within five years, classical methods had closed much of the gap.

claims.title: Quantum Darwinism
claims.standfirst: Why do we and the environment agree about what a measurement found? Quantum Darwinism answers: because the environment keeps many copies, and only some states get copied.

facts.Core idea: Environment selects and copies pointer states
facts.Evidence: Photon and spin experiments show the redundancy structure
facts.Not explained: Why one outcome occurs at all

claims.title: Quantum Healing
claims.standfirst: The claim that consciousness can direct quantum processes to heal the body. It uses the vocabulary of quantum mechanics, and every one of its central assertions contradicts what quantum mechanics says about warm, wet tissue.

facts.Claim: Consciousness directs quantum processes to heal
facts.Obstacle: Decoherence in ~10⁻²⁰ s in warm tissue

claims.title: Quantum Oddities
claims.standfirst: Two of the strangest things physicists have said about electrons and death: you can never experience your own, and there may only be one electron in the universe.

claims.title: Quantum Coherence in Photosynthesis
claims.standfirst: Light-harvesting complexes were reported to sustain quantum coherence for hundreds of femtoseconds. Whether that coherence helps, or is a by-product, is the argument.

facts.Reinterpretation: Much of the signal is vibrational

claims.title: Quantum Tunnelling in Smell
claims.standfirst: The claim that we smell by detecting molecular vibrations through quantum tunnelling, rather than by shape. The evidence is mixed and the debate is live.

claims.title: Quetzalcoatl the Visitor
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A feathered serpent god was recast in the twentieth century as a pale-skinned teacher from overseas. The evidence for the visitor is a sixteenth-century text read backwards.

claims.title: The Quimbaya Aeroplanes
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Small gold figurines from Colombia have triangular wings and a vertical tail. Replicas have been flown as gliders, which is the argument, and the argument is backwards.

claims.title: Ragnarök and 536 AD
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A volcanic winter darkened the sun for eighteen months, and Norse legend describes a winter with no summer. The parallel is suggestive.

claims.title: The Rainbow Warrior
claims.standfirst: French intelligence officers sank a Greenpeace ship in Auckland harbour, killing a photographer. France initially denied it, then admitted it.

facts.Perpetrator: French DGSE, authorised at ministerial level

claims.title: Raining Animals
claims.standfirst: Reports of fish, frogs and other animals falling from the sky are documented across centuries. The mechanism is meteorological, and it is well understood.

facts.Pattern: Single species, near a water body

claims.title: Rama Setu
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka, sacred in one account and a natural feature in another.

claims.title: Randonautica
claims.standfirst: An app that generates a random coordinate and sends you there, promising 'anomalies'. In 2020 two teenagers following one found a suitcase containing human remains, and the app became famous for the wrong reason.

facts.Famous case: A suitcase found in Washington state, 2020

claims.title: Rare Earth or Mediocrity
claims.standfirst: Is complex life rare because Earth is unusual, or ordinary because the galaxy is vast? Both arguments are principled and neither is settled.

claims.title: Rational Choice Voting
claims.standfirst: Downs noticed in 1957 that a self-interested voter should stay home. Sixty years of research has produced four kinds of answer, and no consensus on which one describes actual voters.

facts.Unresolved: Which explanation is the true one

claims.title: Readiness Potentials and Free Will
claims.standfirst: In 1983 Benjamin Libet measured a slow build-up of brain activity starting a few hundred milliseconds before subjects reported deciding to move. It has been cited as proof that free will is an illusion ever since.

claims.title: Reality Shifting
claims.standfirst: A practice, spread on TikTok, of moving consciousness to another reality by relaxing into sleep. It is a description of dreaming with a different vocabulary and a stronger claim.

claims.title: The Referee Who Bet
claims.standfirst: Match officials have bet on games and, in some cases, influenced them. The cases are documented in court and league records.

claims.title: Relational Quantum Mechanics
claims.standfirst: The proposal that quantum states are always relative to an observer, and that there is no observer-independent description.

claims.title: Rendering Optimisation
claims.standfirst: The claim that reality only renders what is observed, as a game engine does. The observation is real; the engine is a metaphor.

claims.title: The Replication Crisis
claims.standfirst: Large numbers of published findings in psychology and medicine failed to replicate. The failure is documented, and so are its causes.

facts.Causes: Small samples; flexible analysis; publication bias

claims.title: Repressed Memory
claims.standfirst: The claim that traumatic memories can be pushed out of awareness and recovered later, often in therapy. The evidence for the mechanism is weak, and the recovered memories have produced both convictions and miscarriages of justice.

facts.Lab finding: Suggestions can create confident false memories

claims.title: The Resource Curse
claims.standfirst: Saudi Arabia and Nigeria both sit on enormous oil reserves. One has a GDP per head around twenty times the other. The difference is not geology.

claims.title: Retrocausality
claims.standfirst: The proposal that later events can influence earlier ones. Some interpretations use it; no experiment has shown it.

claims.title: Richard III Under a Car Park
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The last Plantagenet king was buried in a friary that became a car park. His skeleton was found in 2012, under a marked parking bay.

claims.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
claims.standfirst: One vertical line in the complex plane decides how evenly the primes are spread. Ten trillion zeros agree. Nobody can prove it, and nobody serious thinks it is false.

claims.title: RLHF
claims.standfirst: The technique that turned raw models into assistants, and the argument about what it actually does.

claims.title: RNA World or Metabolism First
claims.standfirst: Two answers to how life began: a self-replicating molecule, or a self-sustaining chemical network. Both have support and neither is demonstrated.

claims.title: The Lost Colony
claims.standfirst: 115 English colonists, a word carved on a post, and four centuries of stories about vanishing. The likeliest answer is that they did not vanish at all.

claims.title: The Robbers Cave Experiment
claims.standfirst: Two groups of boys at a summer camp were set against each other. The conflict and the reconciliation are both documented.

claims.title: Roko's Basilisk
claims.standfirst: A future AI will torture anyone who knew it was coming and did nothing to help. You have now read about it. That last sentence is the entire mechanism.

facts.Named after: The basilisk — kills by being seen

claims.title: Roman Concrete That Heals
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Roman marine concrete has survived two thousand years of seawater. The explanation is lime clasts that crack, dissolve and recrystallise — and a 2023 study found a way to make it deliberately.

facts.2023 study: MIT: the clasts were deliberate; a modern version heals

claims.title: Roman Dodecahedrons
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Hollow bronze objects with twelve pentagonal faces and knobs at the corners, found across the northern provinces. Nobody knows what they were for.

claims.title: Rome Traded with India
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Roman coins are found in India, and a Roman-era text describes the monsoon route. The trade was large enough to worry Roman writers.

claims.title: Rongorongo
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A script from Easter Island, carved on wooden tablets, and undeciphered. Only about two dozen objects survive.

claims.title: Room 641A
claims.standfirst: A room in an AT&T switching centre in San Francisco, built for the NSA, where internet traffic was copied. A technician's evidence exposed it in 2006.

facts.Later: Confirmed in outline by the 2013 disclosures

claims.title: The Rosenhan Study
claims.standfirst: Healthy people admitted to psychiatric hospitals and diagnosed. The study reshaped psychiatry and its data have been questioned.

claims.title: Roswell Was Project Mogul
claims.standfirst: The 1947 Roswell debris was a secret balloon array built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The US Air Force said so in 1994, and the alien story arrived decades later.

claims.title: Rothschild Banking Myths
claims.standfirst: A family of bankers has been at the centre of conspiracy theories for two centuries. The theories are documented as theories, and they are false — and they repeat a familiar pattern of antisemitic tropes.

claims.title: The Roza Bal Tomb
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A shrine in Srinagar said to be a prophet's tomb. The identification is modern, and the site's own tradition is different.

claims.title: The Russian Sleep Experiment
claims.standfirst: A creepypasta about a Soviet experiment that kept prisoners awake for fifteen days. It is written as a report and it is entirely invented.

claims.title: Sad Satan
claims.standfirst: A 2015 horror game distributed through the deep web, said to contain illegal material. The claims are unverified, the game has been examined, and its authorship is unknown.

facts.Medium: A game file passed between users

claims.title: Sai Baba's Miracles
claims.standfirst: A figure credited with materialising objects and knowing the future. The claims are testimony; the demonstrations are not testable.

claims.title: The Sailing Stones
claims.standfirst: Rocks on a dry lake bed leave long tracks, apparently moving on their own. The explanation — ice sheets pushed by light wind — was confirmed with GPS and time-lapse in 2014.

facts.Mechanism: Floating ice sheets pushed by wind

claims.title: Saki Sanobashi
claims.standfirst: A lost anime said to show children trapped in a bathroom. It has never been found, and the search suggests it never existed.

claims.title: Salting Carthage
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, and the story says the ground was sown with salt so nothing would grow. The salt is a modern invention.

claims.title: The Sanjeevani Plant
claims.standfirst: A life-restoring herb from the Ramayana, and a long search for its botanical identity.

claims.title: The Saqqara Bird
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A wooden bird from an Egyptian tomb, about 2,200 years old, was said to be a model glider. It has no tail fin, no airfoil, and no evidence of ever having flown.

facts.Missing for flight: Tail fin, wing camber, sufficient wing area

claims.title: The Saraswati River
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A river praised in the Vedas and identified by some with a dry channel in Haryana. The palaeochannel is real; the identification is argued.

claims.title: Satoshi as an Intelligence Agency
claims.standfirst: The claim that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator was a state intelligence operation. The identity is unknown, and the claim is an inference from the design.

claims.title: Saturated Fat
claims.standfirst: The central claim of modern dietary advice, and the subject of a long, documented argument.

claims.title: The Savant Reservoir
claims.standfirst: The claim that everyone carries a hidden savant inside, unlocked by injury or effort. Acquired savant syndrome is real; the reservoir is an inference with nothing behind it.

facts.The reservoir claim: Latent in everyone — no mechanism, no measure

claims.title: Scaling Laws
claims.standfirst: Double the parameters and the loss drops by a predictable amount, across seven orders of magnitude. Then the awkward part: loss is not capability, and the smooth curves stop being smooth.

facts.Established: Power-law loss in parameters, data, compute (2020)

claims.title: Scarcity or Ingenuity
claims.standfirst: The bet was $1,000 on five metals over ten years. Simon won, Ehrlich paid, and the argument has continued as if the bet had not happened.

facts.Long-run trend: Falling real prices for most minerals

claims.title: SCP-096
claims.standfirst: A fictional creature that becomes violently distressed when its face is seen. It is one entry in a collaborative writing project with thousands of them, and it is labelled fiction everywhere it appears.

claims.title: SCP Is a Real Agency
claims.standfirst: The SCP Foundation is a collaborative fiction wiki. The claim that it is a real agency with real containment procedures is a misunderstanding of a very consistent joke.

claims.title: Screen Time and Teen Mental Health
claims.standfirst: Two camps, one dataset, opposite headlines. The honest summary is that screen use correlates weakly with well-being, that the correlation is smaller than nearly everything else in the same data, and that causality is unresolved.

facts.Trend: Rises in adolescent distress from ≈2012 in several countries
facts.Effect size: Small — smaller than sleep or bullying

claims.title: Who Were the Sea Peoples?
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Egyptian inscriptions record a coalition of peoples attacking the Nile Delta at the end of the Bronze Age. Nobody knows where they came from, and the question is older than archaeology.

facts.Recorded: Merneptah, c. 1208 BC; Ramesses III, c. 1177 BC
facts.Contested: Origins of the rest; one movement or several

claims.title: Secret Societies
claims.standfirst: The Illuminati existed for about ten years, was banned, had its papers seized and published — and has been running the world ever since, according to people who have never read the papers.

facts.Archive: Seized, published, now studied at Erfurt

claims.title: Secret Tests
claims.standfirst: A city sprayed with bacteria, dead infants measured for fallout, a cat with a transmitter in its skull, a gun that causes heart attacks, and a proposal to make soldiers attracted to each other. All real documents.

claims.title: Secular Stagnation
claims.standfirst: If the interest rate that balances saving and investment is below zero, the central bank cannot reach it. Demand then falls short year after year, and the economy runs cool not because of a shock but because of its structure.

claims.title: Seed Oils and Inflammation
claims.standfirst: The claim that industrial seed oils cause inflammation through omega-6 fatty acids. The biochemistry is real; the clinical evidence does not support the harm.

facts.Biochemistry: Linoleic acid to arachidonic acid — real
facts.Cohort data: Higher linoleic acid linked to lower risk

claims.title: Seigniorage
claims.standfirst: The profit from issuing money, and the reason governments can fund themselves by printing.

claims.title: The Serotonin Critique
claims.standfirst: A 2022 umbrella review found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin. The argument since has been about what that means for the drugs, and the drugs still work.

facts.Finding: No consistent evidence for low serotonin
facts.Drug efficacy: Better than placebo in moderate to severe depression
facts.Common misreading: That the drugs do not work

claims.title: Serotonin and Depression
claims.standfirst: The story that depression is caused by low serotonin is the most repeated claim in mental health. A 2022 review found no consistent evidence for it, and the argument since has been about what that means for the drugs.

facts.2022 review: No consistent evidence for lowered serotonin
facts.Drug efficacy: Better than placebo in moderate to severe depression
facts.The harm: A simplification repeated until it was believed

claims.title: The Seven Cities of Gold
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Spanish explorers were told of seven golden cities to the north. Coronado found pueblos of stone and mud, and no gold.

claims.title: The Shadow Biosphere
claims.standfirst: The proposal that life with a different biochemistry exists on Earth, undetected because our methods assume ours. It is a serious hypothesis with one famous failed test.

facts.Claim: Life with a different biochemistry, undetected

claims.title: Who Wrote Shakespeare?
claims.standfirst: A glovemaker's son from Warwickshire could not have written those plays — so runs the argument, and it has been running since 1856. The documents say otherwise, and they are duller than the conspiracy.

claims.title: Shared Dreaming
claims.standfirst: Two people report the same dream on the same night. It is one of the most compelling experiences a person can have and one of the hardest claims to test, because dreams are private and reports are not.

facts.Claim: Two or more people experience the same dream
facts.Obstacle: Dreams are known only through post-waking reports

claims.title: Shaving Makes Hair Thicker
claims.standfirst: Shaving does not change hair growth. The stubble only feels coarser.

claims.title: Short-Form Video and Attention
claims.standfirst: The claim that short-form video has shortened attention spans. The evidence is mixed, the definition of attention is contested, and the platforms measure engagement, not cognition.

facts.Precedent: The same panic for older media

claims.title: Shrinkflation and Skimpflation
claims.standfirst: Products get smaller or worse while the price stays the same. Both are documented by statistics agencies, and both are hard for a shopper to see.

claims.title: The Shroud as a Radiation Flash
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Shroud of Turin is a fourteenth-century linen cloth. The claim that its image was burned in by a burst of radiation at the resurrection explains the image and contradicts the dating, which is the wrong way round.

facts.The circularity: The date is 'reset' by the event the date is used against

claims.title: Silk Road Glass
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Roman and later glass found along Asian trade routes, showing how far goods travelled and how technology spread.

claims.title: The Silo Green Screen
claims.standfirst: A theory that the view outside the silo is a screen. It is an interpretation of a television series.

claims.title: The Silurian Hypothesis
claims.standfirst: If an industrial civilisation lived on Earth 60 million years ago, would we know? Two astrophysicists asked the question properly — and the answer says more about us than about them.

claims.title: The Simian Line and Palmistry
claims.standfirst: One crease across the palm instead of two is a real anatomical variant, more common in some conditions. The claim that it reveals character, destiny or 'simian' ancestry is where it stops being anatomy.

facts.Frequency: A few per cent; normal variant
facts.Associated with: Down syndrome and some developmental conditions
facts.Personality link: None; palm reading tests at chance

claims.title: The Simpsons Predictions
claims.standfirst: The show has run for more than 750 episodes of jokes about the future. People remember the ones that landed. Here is the whole list, checked episode by episode, with the ones that did not land.

claims.title: The Simpsons Time Machine
claims.standfirst: The Simpsons appears to predict events. With nearly 800 episodes over 35 years, some of them will match, and the ones that do are the ones that get posted.

claims.title: The Simulation Hypothesis
claims.standfirst: Bostrom's argument is not “we are probably simulated”. It is a trilemma, and one of the three horns is boring. The internet took the exciting horn and dropped the rest.

claims.title: The Singularity
claims.standfirst: The claim that machine intelligence will improve itself in a runaway loop, and that the curve becomes vertical at some point. It rests on an argument about recursive self-improvement that has never been demonstrated.

claims.title: Skinwalker Ranch
claims.standfirst: A ranch in Utah with a reputation for cattle mutilation, strange lights and 'portals'. It was investigated by a defence contractor and by a television series, with no published findings.

claims.title: Skinwalker Whistling Lore
claims.standfirst: Internet posts claim that whistling at night attracts a skinwalker. The taboo is real in some traditions; the internet version is not.

claims.title: Sleepwalking Violence
claims.standfirst: People have committed violence while asleep, and courts have had to decide what that means.

claims.title: Slender Man as a Tulpa
claims.standfirst: The claim that Slender Man became real because enough people thought about him. He was invented in a forum contest in 2009, and the tulpa claim is part of the fiction.

facts.Creator: Eric Knudsen
facts.Spread: Fiction, video series, a criminal case

claims.title: Smart Cities as Surveillance Grids
claims.standfirst: The claim that smart-city projects are a cover for total surveillance. The sensors are real; the total grid is not, and the projects have mostly been smaller and duller.

claims.title: Smart TV Viewing Surveillance
claims.standfirst: Televisions that recognise what is on screen and report it. The feature is documented in patents, settings and research.

claims.title: Smile.jpg
claims.standfirst: A creepypasta about an image that drives people mad. The image is a story element, and the story is the work.

facts.Format: A story about a cursed image

claims.title: The Smiling Man
claims.standfirst: A creepypasta about a man in a suit who dances in the street at night. It is fiction, and it is one of the genre's best-known short pieces.

claims.title: Snowball Earth
claims.standfirst: Twice in the Neoproterozoic, ice reached sea level in the tropics. The evidence is in the rocks and is not seriously disputed; how the planet got out again is still argued about.

facts.Mechanism: Ice–albedo runaway, ended by volcanic CO₂
facts.Open question: Hard snowball or open equatorial water

claims.title: Sodom and the Airburst
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A 2021 paper argued that a site in Jordan was destroyed by a Tunguska-like airburst around 1650 BC, and linked it to Sodom. The claim is contested on chronology, geology and identification.

claims.title: The Sokal Hoax
claims.standfirst: A physicist submitted a deliberately absurd paper to a cultural-studies journal, and it was published.

claims.title: Solar Geoengineering
claims.standfirst: Cooling the planet by reflecting sunlight — sulphate aerosols in the stratosphere, or brighter clouds. The physics is understood, the governance is not, and the termination problem is the argument against.

facts.Key risks: Termination shock; no effect on acidification

claims.title: Soma
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A ritual drink praised in the Rigveda, and a botanical identification that has never been settled.

claims.title: The Somerton Man
claims.standfirst: A man found dead on an Adelaide beach in 1948, with a scrap of Persian poetry and an unbreakable code. He was identified by DNA in 2022.

claims.title: Sonoluminescence
claims.standfirst: Sound makes a bubble collapse; the collapse emits a flash of light lasting picoseconds. The inside may be hotter than the surface of the Sun, and nobody can measure it directly.

claims.title: Sony's Rootkit
claims.standfirst: Music CDs installed hidden software that compromised the computers of the people who bought them.

claims.title: The Electromagnetic Soul
claims.standfirst: “The soul is an electromagnetic pattern; the body is hardware.” It sounds like physics. It is a metaphor wearing a lab coat — and the real measurements are more interesting than the metaphor.

facts.Fatal step: Fields are a product, not the mind

claims.title: The Sovereign Strawman
claims.standfirst: The claim that a birth certificate creates a corporate 'strawman' separate from the real person, and that a living soul can escape law by naming it. Courts have rejected it in every jurisdiction that has heard it.

facts.Claim: A birth certificate creates a separate legal entity

claims.title: The Space Elevator
claims.standfirst: Tsiolkovsky proposed it in 1895 after seeing the Eiffel Tower. Arthur C. Clarke made it famous in 1979. It remains the cheapest imaginable way to orbit and the least available, for one reason: the material.

claims.title: The Spear of Destiny
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A spear said to have pierced Christ, and a legend that its holder commands the world. The legend is modern.

claims.title: Water Erosion on the Sphinx
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Sphinx's enclosure shows deep vertical weathering. Whether that pattern is rain, salt, wind or groundwater decides how old the monument is, and the argument has been running since 1979.

facts.Claim: Rainfall erosion implies an older date
facts.Mainstream reading: Salt exfoliation, wind, groundwater, joint-controlled fissures
facts.Complication: Centuries of burial, excavation and repair
facts.What would settle it: A survey separating original surface from repairs

claims.title: Spinosaurus Lifestyle
claims.standfirst: A dinosaur with a sail, a crocodile snout and dense bones, proposed as a swimmer. The 2020 tail find supported it; later work questioned whether it could dive.

claims.title: The Splinternet
claims.standfirst: The internet is fragmenting into national and regional blocs, with different rules, different infrastructure and different content. It is measurable, and the measurement is the interesting part.

claims.title: Split-Brain Consciousness
claims.standfirst: Severing the connection between the hemispheres produced patients whose two halves seemed to know different things. Whether that means two minds is still argued.

claims.title: Squid Game Card Colours
claims.standfirst: A fan theory holds that the red and blue cards in Squid Game encode the choice between the games and the outside world. The show's creator has described the cards more simply.

claims.title: Stairs in the Woods
claims.standfirst: A creepypasta about flights of stairs found in forests, leading nowhere. It began as an imageboard thread and became a genre fixture.

claims.title: The Stanford Prison Experiment
claims.standfirst: The most famous psychology experiment ever run, and the one with the most documented problems.

claims.title: Star Jelly
claims.standfirst: A gelatinous substance found in fields, traditionally said to fall from the sky during meteor showers. The DNA work has found frog and toad, and the rest is slime mould and bacteria.

claims.title: The Star of Bethlehem
claims.standfirst: Matthew mentions a star that led the Magi to Bethlehem. Astronomy has offered conjunctions, comets and supernovae, and none of them fits the text without strain.

claims.title: Starlink and UFO Panics
claims.standfirst: A train of bright lights crosses the sky, and a town reports a UFO. It is a line of satellites catching the sun, and the reports are now a routine part of astronomy outreach.

facts.Cause: Satellites in a line, sunlit after sunset

claims.title: Stepwells
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Buildings that descend to the water table, and the engineering that made them work in a monsoon climate.

claims.title: Stereotype Threat
claims.standfirst: The claim that reminding people of a negative stereotype about their group impairs their performance. It replicated in small studies and largely failed in large pre-registered ones.

claims.title: Sterile Neutrinos
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A hypothetical neutrino that interacts only through gravity. Several anomalies pointed to it; the experiments have not confirmed it.

claims.title: Stevie Wonder Can See
claims.standfirst: A claim that a blind musician is not blind. It is a joke that has been repeated as fact.

claims.title: Stochastic Parrots or World Models
claims.standfirst: One camp says a language model is a curve-fitting machine that parrots its training data. The other says that to predict text well enough, it has to build a model of the world that produced it.

facts.Strongest evidence for structure: Board-state probes in chess and Othello models
facts.Open question: How general the learned representations are

claims.title: Stone Softening in the Andes
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that Inca masons softened stone with plant acids to fit it perfectly. The fit is real; the method is not established.

claims.title: The Stoned Ape
claims.standfirst: Human brains tripled in size because our ancestors ate psilocybin mushrooms, which rewired us into language, art and self-reflection. It is a wonderful story with a real pharmacology and almost no archaeology.

claims.title: Stonehenge Acoustics
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A replica of Stonehenge has been built and measured. The stones do affect sound in ways that would matter for speech, music and drumming — and the site is a ruin, which is the problem with every claim about how it sounded.

facts.The problem: The site is a ruin; reconstructions differ
facts.Unresolved: Whether any acoustic effect was intended

claims.title: Stonehenge as a Computer
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: In 1963 an astronomer argued that Stonehenge was a machine for predicting eclipses. The alignments are real; the machine is the part that did not survive scrutiny.

facts.Claim: An observatory and an eclipse predictor
facts.Problem: 165 points produce thousands of chance alignments

claims.title: The Streisand Effect
claims.standfirst: An attempt to suppress information draws attention to it. The name comes from a photograph of a house, and the mechanism is now a standard part of online strategy.

claims.title: Strings versus Loops
claims.standfirst: Two research programmes, one target: a theory of gravity that works at the Planck scale. They disagree about almost everything else, and neither has been tested.

claims.title: Stuxnet
claims.standfirst: A computer worm that destroyed uranium centrifuges in Iran by making them spin at the wrong speed while reporting normal operation. It is the first known cyber weapon to cause physical damage.

facts.Target: Siemens controllers at an enrichment plant
facts.Technique: Replay normal data while damaging centrifuges

claims.title: Sub-Simulation Stacking
claims.standfirst: The claim that simulations nest inside simulations, so that our world is many layers down. The argument is statistical, and it has no empirical content.

claims.title: Substrate Independence
claims.standfirst: Functionalism says a mind is defined by what it does, not what it is made of — so the same program would be conscious wherever it ran. That is either obvious or a category error, and the disagreement is about which.

claims.title: Succession as King Lear
claims.standfirst: The comparison between the Roy family and Shakespeare's tragedy is made constantly. It is a useful reading and it is not a hidden source.

claims.title: Sugar and Hyperactivity
claims.standfirst: Sugar does not make children hyperactive. Parents and blinded observers disagree, and that is the finding.

claims.title: Sundaland
claims.standfirst: A drowned subcontinent in Southeast Asia, exposed at low sea levels, with a coastline the size of Europe's. It is real; what happened on it is the debate.

claims.title: Dual Suns, Dual Stars
claims.standfirst: The Sun has no companion today. That is a measurement, not an opinion — and yet the “second sun” idea is one of the most persistent in fringe cosmology, because it is half right.

claims.title: Room-Temperature Superconductivity
claims.standfirst: A material that carries current with no resistance would rebuild the electrical grid. The physics is real; the room-temperature claims have not survived.

claims.title: Superdeterminism
claims.standfirst: The proposal that quantum experiments violate Bell's inequalities because the settings were fixed in advance. It saves locality and gives up free choice.

facts.Claim: Settings are correlated with hidden variables

claims.title: Superintelligence
claims.standfirst: The proposal that an intelligence explosion would produce a system beyond human control. The argument is documented; the outcome is speculative.

claims.title: The Superman Curse
claims.standfirst: Actors associated with Superman are said to suffer misfortune. The list is long because the franchise is long.

claims.title: Superrationality
claims.standfirst: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma with a stranger, defecting is dominant. Unless the stranger is your mirror — in which case the choice is not what to do, but what kind of reasoner to be.

facts.Key assumption: Both players run the same reasoning
facts.Descendants: Evidential, timeless and functional decision theory

claims.title: Supersymmetry
claims.standfirst: A symmetry between matter and force particles would solve several problems at once. The LHC was built partly to find it, and has found nothing. That is not the same as ruling it out.

claims.title: Sushruta's Surgery
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A Sanskrit surgical text describing operations including rhinoplasty. The text is real and its procedures were performed.

claims.title: Sweet Potatoes Crossed the Pacific
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A South American crop was being grown in Polynesia before Europeans arrived. Someone crossed the ocean with it.

claims.title: Swimming After Eating
claims.standfirst: The rule that you must wait an hour after eating before swimming. There is no evidence for it.

claims.title: Jung's Synchronicity
claims.standfirst: A meaningful coincidence with no causal connection, offered as an acausal principle of nature. The concept names something people experience; as a claim about the world it cannot be tested, which is the problem.

facts.Testability: None — meaning is assigned after the fact
facts.Base rate: Coincidences are common; that is arithmetic

claims.title: Synesthesia
claims.standfirst: For some people, letters have colours and sounds have tastes, consistently, for a lifetime. It is one of the few claims in this archive that a laboratory can check in an afternoon.

facts.Mechanism: Contested; reduced neonatal pruning is the leading account

claims.title: Tabby’s Star
claims.standfirst: A star 1,470 light years away keeps dimming in strange, uneven ways. A comet swarm was the first guess, dust the current one — and a megastructure was never more than a headline.

claims.title: Tachyons
claims.standfirst: Particles that always travel faster than light. They are mathematically possible and physically absent.

claims.title: Tardigrades Between Planets
claims.standfirst: A millimetre-long animal that survives vacuum, radiation and decades without water is real. The claim built on top of it — that life travels between planets — is a different proposition, and the experiments that get quoted do not support it.

facts.Tun state: Metabolism below measurement; DNA repaired on rehydration
facts.Space test: 2007, low Earth orbit, ten days, survivors
facts.Panspermia: Not demonstrated; the transit dose is the problem

claims.title: Tartaria & the Mud Flood
claims.standfirst: Every old city has basement windows cut in half by the pavement. The theory says a civilisation of giants built the buildings, then a wall of mud buried the ground floors and the history books.

facts.\u201cTartary\u201d in fact: European label for inner Asia — not an empire
facts.Core evidence: Buried ground floors, fair buildings, star forts
facts.Real explanation: Street regrading, temporary exhibition halls, bastion geometry

claims.title: Tartarus, the Pit
claims.standfirst: “As far beneath the earth as heaven is above it.” The Greeks gave the underworld a floor plan, a wall, a gate and a prisoner list. Everything after that is reuse.

facts.Depth: Nine days and nights of falling
facts.Inmates: The Titans; Typhoeus; later, human sinners

claims.title: Tartessos
claims.standfirst: A wealthy kingdom in southern Spain, described by Greek writers, that traded with the Phoenicians and then vanished. Its capital has never been found.

facts.Trade: Silver and tin, with the Phoenicians

claims.title: The Taylor Swift Clone
claims.standfirst: A claim that a celebrity has been replaced by a double. It is the oldest rumour in fandom, applied to a new subject.

claims.title: The Tecaxic Head
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A small stone head found in Mexico with features said to be Roman. The object is real; its origin is disputed.

claims.title: Technofeudalism
claims.standfirst: The claim that cloud platforms have replaced markets with rents, and that capitalism has been succeeded by something older in structure. It is a thesis about political economy, argued from data that is contested.

facts.Claim: Cloud platforms extract rent; capitalism has been succeeded
facts.Contested: Rent versus profit as the description
facts.Missing: Evidence that a new mode of production exists

claims.title: Technological Unemployment
claims.standfirst: Every generation has been told that machines will end work, and every generation has been mostly wrong. That history is an argument, not a guarantee.

facts.Current AI evidence: Task-level gains; no clear aggregate effect yet
facts.Key variable: Whether new tasks are created for people

claims.title: Technosignature Pollution
claims.standfirst: The idea that a civilisation could be detected by its pollution — nitrogen dioxide, chlorofluorocarbons, industrial waste — rather than by its radio.

claims.title: The Technosphere Layer
claims.standfirst: The claim that human technology has become a geological layer of the planet, with its own mass and dynamics. The concept is now used in Earth-systems science.

claims.title: Ted the Caver
claims.standfirst: A caving diary posted online in 2001, in which a narrow passage leads to something. It is one of the oldest creepypastas, and it was written as fiction.

claims.title: The Telephone and Deafness
claims.standfirst: Early telephones were said to damage hearing and cause 'telephone deafness'. The claim did not survive measurement.

claims.title: The Ten Per Cent Brain
claims.standfirst: The claim that we use a tenth of our brains. Imaging shows activity throughout.

claims.title: Mercury Under Teotihuacan
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Liquid mercury was found in a tunnel under the Feathered Serpent pyramid. It is documented, and it is not evidence of anything exotic.

claims.title: The Terracotta Army
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Thousands of life-size soldiers buried with the First Emperor, individually modelled and painted, found by farmers digging a well.

claims.title: Earth Was Terraformed
claims.standfirst: The claim that Earth was engineered for life — by an earlier civilisation, or by design. It borrows the language of a real scientific debate about fine-tuning and rare Earth, and then adds an agent nobody has evidence for.

claims.title: Terror Management Theory
claims.standfirst: The claim that awareness of death drives people toward cultural worldviews and self-esteem. It has hundreds of studies behind it, a replication problem, and a large theoretical apparatus.

claims.title: The Tetris Effect
claims.standfirst: Play Tetris for hours and the falling blocks follow you into sleep and into the shower. The effect is real, it has a name, and it turned out to be a window on how memory consolidates.

facts.Finding: Imagery at sleep onset, in most intensive players

claims.title: Tetris as a Soviet Weapon
claims.standfirst: A joke that the Soviet Union built Tetris as a psychological weapon. It was written by a programmer in 1984, and it was not.

claims.title: The Amplituhedron
claims.standfirst: A geometric object whose volume encodes particle-scattering probabilities. It works, and it is not yet physics in the usual sense.

claims.title: The Elevator Tape
claims.standfirst: A surveillance clip said to show something impossible in a lift. The clip exists; the reading does not follow.

claims.title: The Overton Window
claims.standfirst: The range of policies a public will accept, and how it shifts. It is a description, not a conspiracy.

claims.title: The Strange Man
claims.standfirst: A creepypasta figure who appears in the background of photographs. The story is fiction, and the photographs are props.

claims.title: The Third Place
claims.standfirst: The claim that cafés, bars, parks and barbers are the places where community actually forms, and that they are disappearing. The concept is well formed; the decline is harder to measure.

claims.title: Theranos
claims.standfirst: One drop of blood, two hundred tests, a black box. The machine did not work, the tests ran on other companies' equipment, and the board did not include a single haematologist.

facts.Claim: 200+ tests from one drop of blood
facts.Reality: Few tests; most run on commercial analysers

claims.title: The Three Men Ghost Boy
claims.standfirst: A figure in a window in Three Men and a Baby was said to be a dead boy. It is a cardboard cutout of one of the actors.

facts.Reality: A cardboard cutout of Ted Danson

claims.title: The Thucydides Trap
claims.standfirst: Thucydides said the war between Athens and Sparta came from 'the growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta'. Allison turned that sentence into a dataset.

claims.title: Thule
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A Greek navigator described a land six days' sail north of Britain, where the sea became sluggish. Nobody knows which land he meant.

facts.Clue: Six days' sail; a sluggish sea

claims.title: Thunderbirds
claims.standfirst: Giant birds in Native American tradition and in a famous photograph that turned out to be a hoax. The tradition is real; the bird is not.

facts.Key evidence: A photograph, since shown to be a hoax

claims.title: The Tic Tac
claims.standfirst: A Navy pilot filmed an object off San Diego in 2004 that looked like a tic tac and appeared to move impossibly. It is the best-documented modern UAP case, and it is still unexplained.

claims.title: TikTok as Psychological Warfare
claims.standfirst: A claim that a platform is a weapon aimed at a population. The platform is real and its effects are studied; the warfare framing is not established.

claims.title: Time Crystals
claims.standfirst: An ordinary crystal repeats in space. A time crystal repeats in time, indefinitely, without consuming energy — and unlike a pendulum, it does so in its ground state.

facts.Driven?: Yes — a discrete time crystal needs a drive

claims.title: Time Paradoxes
claims.standfirst: Kill your grandfather and you were never born; travel back and give yourself the idea you got from yourself. These paradoxes are not puzzles about fiction. They are what happens when you take the equations of relativity seriously.

claims.title: Timewave Zero
claims.standfirst: A curve derived from the I Ching, claimed to map the novelty of the universe and to end in 2012. The date passed; the curve was fitted, not derived.

facts.Basis: The King Wen sequence of the I Ching
facts.Outcome: No event; no revision into a testable claim
facts.Method: A curve with free parameters, fitted to history

claims.title: Tired Light
claims.standfirst: Redshift could be caused by photons losing energy on the way, rather than by the expansion of space. It was a serious alternative for sixty years, and three measurements have closed it.

facts.Claim: Redshift is photon energy loss in transit
facts.Killed by: Time dilation, the CMB, surface brightness
facts.Why it persists: It would remove the Big Bang

claims.title: The Titanic–Olympic Switch
claims.standfirst: A claim that the Titanic was swapped with its sister ship for the insurance. The ships' records settle it.

facts.Evidence against: Hull numbers; photographs; plans; the wreck

claims.title: The Toba Catastrophe
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A supereruption in Sumatra and a theory that it nearly ended humanity. The eruption is documented; the bottleneck is contested.

claims.title: The Tongue Map
claims.standfirst: The diagram showing sweetness at the tip and bitterness at the back. It came from a mistranslation and it is wrong.

claims.title: Toon Force
claims.standfirst: The convention that cartoon characters obey comedy rather than physics. It is a description of a genre rule, not a claim about anything.

claims.title: Trepanation
claims.standfirst: Boring a hole in a living skull, done for millennia, and sometimes survived.

claims.title: T. rex the Scavenger
claims.standfirst: The claim that Tyrannosaurus was too slow and too small-eyed to hunt, and lived as a scavenger. The evidence points to an animal that did both.

claims.title: Trickle-Down Economics
claims.standfirst: A nickname for supply-side tax cuts, and a claim about who benefits. The evidence is contested and the term is a slogan.

claims.title: The Trillion-Dollar Coin
claims.standfirst: A legal loophole proposed in 2011 to bypass a debt-ceiling standoff. The proposal is documented; it was never used.

claims.title: The Trojan Horse as a Ram
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A proposal that the 'horse' was a siege engine or a ship's figurehead rather than a wooden animal. The poem says horse; the archaeology says siege.

claims.title: Troy Was Real
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The city in the Iliad was treated as fiction until a German businessman dug up a mound in Turkey. The site is real; the war is another question.

claims.title: The Truman Show Delusion
claims.standfirst: A delusion in which the patient believes their life is a television show and everyone around them is acting. It is documented, it is rare, and it is named after a film.

facts.Status: A description, not a new syndrome
facts.Content: Life as a broadcast; others as actors

claims.title: Tryptophan and Turkey
claims.standfirst: The claim that turkey makes you sleepy. Turkey has no more tryptophan than chicken, and the meal is the cause.

facts.Cause: Meal size; alcohol; time of day

claims.title: Tulpas
claims.standfirst: A practice imported from Tibetan Buddhism and rebuilt on internet forums: deliberately create a second mind in your head, and talk to it. The reports are real; the claim that there is a second mind is not testable.

facts.Reports: A voice with its own opinions; sometimes distress

claims.title: Turbulence
claims.standfirst: We can land a rocket on a barge using models of turbulent flow. We cannot prove that the equations describing it always have smooth solutions.

claims.title: The Turing Test
claims.standfirst: Turing's 1950 paper replaced an unanswerable question with a game: can a machine's text be told from a person's? Seventy-five years later the game is won and the original question is exactly where it was.

facts.Turing's prediction: Machine fools an average interrogator by ≈2000
facts.What it tests: Fluency and human modelling, not understanding

claims.title: The Turtle's Shell
claims.standfirst: A turtle's shell is its ribcage, grown outward and fused. How that happened without killing the animal is the question, and the fossil record has narrowed it.

facts.Structure: Ribs and vertebrae fused into bone

claims.title: Hidden Chambers in Tut's Tomb
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that Nefertiti's tomb lies behind the walls of Tutankhamun's burial chamber, based on radar scans. The scans were repeated, and the chambers were not there.

claims.title: Tutankhamun's Meteorite Dagger
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A dagger buried with Tutankhamun was made of iron that fell from the sky. It took ninety years and an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer to prove what the nickel content had hinted at.

facts.Significance: Iron before the Iron Age came from meteorites

claims.title: The Twin Prime Conjecture
claims.standfirst: There are infinitely many pairs of primes two apart. Nobody can prove it, though we now know there are infinitely many pairs at some fixed distance.

facts.Statement: Infinitely many prime pairs differing by 2

claims.title: The Twitter Files
claims.standfirst: Internal documents released by a new owner, describing moderation decisions. Their content and their framing are both documented.

claims.title: Type 3 Diabetes
claims.standfirst: The claim that Alzheimer's is a form of diabetes in the brain, driven by insulin resistance. The mechanism is real; the label is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis.

claims.title: Uber's Greyball
claims.standfirst: Software that showed a different version of the app to regulators and to people the company wanted to avoid.

facts.Function: Show regulators a false app view

claims.title: Ulcers Are Bacterial
claims.standfirst: Stomach ulcers were said to be caused by stress and acid. Two Australian researchers found a bacterium living in the stomach lining, were ignored for a decade, and won the Nobel Prize.

claims.title: The Uncanny Valley
claims.standfirst: The claim that near-human figures provoke discomfort before realism is reached. The intuition is widespread; the experimental evidence is mixed.

claims.title: Underwater Worlds
claims.standfirst: More than two-thirds of the seafloor has no modern high-resolution map. That single fact powers an industry of undersea-civilization claims — and it is also the most honest fact on this page.

facts.Related: Inner oceans, Lake monsters, Bermuda Triangle

claims.title: Unexplained Phenomena
claims.standfirst: The honest cases. Not ghosts and not cover-ups — events with real evidence, real papers, and conclusions that are still argued.

claims.title: Unfavorable Semicircle
claims.standfirst: A YouTube channel that uploaded tens of thousands of silent, cryptic videos. It stopped, and nobody has explained it.

claims.title: Universal Basic Income
claims.standfirst: The strongest argument for a basic income is not that it makes people work more. It is that a welfare state built on conditions and paperwork produces the poverty it claims to fix.

facts.Trials: Finland, Kenya, Stockton, Denver, and dozens more
facts.Employment effect: Small in most trials; not the collapse predicted

claims.title: Universal Grammar
claims.standfirst: The claim that children are born with an innate language faculty that constrains the possible grammars. It reshaped linguistics, and the evidence for the strong version has weakened.

claims.title: The Upside Down Time-Freeze
claims.standfirst: A theory that the other dimension in Stranger Things is frozen in 1983. It is an interpretation of a work of fiction.

claims.title: Urban Legends & Creepypasta
claims.standfirst: A Photoshop contest produced a monster. Five years later, two twelve-year-olds tried to kill their friend for him. This is the only page in the archive where the fiction caused the harm.

claims.title: The Vaimanika Shastra
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A twentieth-century Sanskrit text describing flying machines. It was written in this century, not in antiquity.

claims.title: Valhalla as Coping
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A claim that Norse afterlife imagery was a psychological mechanism for warrior societies. The texts are real; the function is a reading.

claims.title: Varsity Blues
claims.standfirst: A college admissions scandal in which wealthy parents paid for fraudulent athletic recruitment. The case is documented in indictments and convictions.

claims.title: Vault-Tec Started the War
claims.standfirst: The Fallout games imply that the corporation behind the survival vaults knew the war was coming, and may have caused it. The evidence is inside the games.

facts.Ambiguous: Whether the company caused the war

claims.title: The Velocity of Money
claims.standfirst: How fast money circulates, and why its apparent collapse puzzled economists.

claims.title: Vents or Ponds
claims.standfirst: Where did the first chemistry happen: deep-sea vents, warm ponds, or somewhere else? Each setting has a case.

claims.title: Life in Venus's Clouds
claims.standfirst: The surface of Venus is hot enough to melt lead. Fifty kilometres up, the pressure and temperature are almost Earth-like — which is why the cloud layer keeps being proposed as a habitat, and why the phosphine claim of 2020 mattered.

facts.Droplets: 75–96% sulfuric acid; very low water activity
facts.Reanalysis: SO₂ and artefacts; abundance at most a trace

claims.title: The Vibrator as a Medical Device
claims.standfirst: An electric appliance sold to doctors for a diagnosis that no longer exists. The history is documented and often exaggerated.

claims.title: The Video Nasties
claims.standfirst: A list of films prosecuted in Britain, and the moral panic that produced it.

claims.title: Vimanas
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Flying machines described in Sanskrit epics, read as aircraft. The texts describe palaces and chariots, and the reading is modern.

claims.title: The Vinland Map
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: A fifteenth-century map showing Vinland looked like proof that the Norse reached America before Columbus. The ink turned out to contain a pigment that was not manufactured until the 1920s.

facts.Decisive finding: Anatase (TiO₂) in the industrial form, in the ink
facts.Norse contact: Still established — by L'Anse aux Meadows

claims.title: The Viral Trigger for Schizophrenia
claims.standfirst: Infections in pregnancy are associated with schizophrenia in the child, and the immune system is implicated. The effect is real and small.

claims.title: Where Viruses Came From
claims.standfirst: Viruses are not alive by most definitions, and they are the most abundant biological entities on Earth. Where they came from is one of biology's genuinely unresolved questions.

claims.title: Vitamin C and Linus Pauling
claims.standfirst: A double Nobel laureate claimed high-dose vitamin C treats cancer and colds. The trials did not agree.

claims.title: Voice Identification
claims.standfirst: Recognising a voice is something people do well and can do badly under stress.

claims.title: Voynich Alien Botany
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: The Voynich manuscript's plants do not match any known species, which has been read as evidence of an alien or otherworldly origin. The plants are drawings in a medieval herbal tradition.

claims.title: Voynich as a Cathar Text
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: One of many proposed readings of the Voynich manuscript: that it is a Cathar or heretical text. The manuscript is real; the reading is not established.

claims.title: The Voynich Manuscript
claims.standfirst: An illustrated book in an unknown script, written on vellum dated to the early fifteenth century. Every generation produces a decipherment. None has survived contact with other scholars.

claims.title: The Walking Moai
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: How were the Easter Island statues moved? A 2012 experiment showed they can be 'walked' upright with ropes, which matches the island's oral tradition.

facts.Statues: Hundreds, up to tens of tonnes

claims.title: WALL-E Cannibalism
claims.standfirst: A joke theory that the humans on the Axiom are being fed to each other. The film shows a food dispenser, not a body.

facts.Theory: The humans are fed recycled dead

claims.title: The Wandjina
claims.theme: The ancient world, myth and archaeology
claims.standfirst: Rock art from the Kimberley shows figures with large white faces and haloes. They were read as astronauts in helmets. They are ancestral beings, painted by the people who still paint them.

facts.The error: Modern iconography imposed on unfamiliar art

claims.title: The Warburg Effect
claims.standfirst: Cancer cells ferment glucose even when oxygen is available. Whether that is a cause of cancer or a consequence is the argument, and the difference matters for treatment.

claims.title: The Watcher House
claims.standfirst: A family bought a house in New Jersey and received letters from someone calling himself 'The Watcher'. The letters are documented; the author is not.
